title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Replace combinational 32-bit DIV/REM and triple multiplier with a 33-cycle radix-2 divider and one shared multiplier
motivation:
The baseline closes at only 5.44 MHz (worst path 199.8 ns, 156 cells, clock_ibuf >
u_fwd > u_ex > u_alu) and uses 12.3k LUT4. The worst path runs through alu.sv, which
builds a fully combinational 32-bit signed/unsigned `/` and `%` (four 32-stage
subtract/compare chains, ~200 ns on Gowin LUT4 fabric) and three separate 32x32->64
multipliers (mul_ss, mul_uu, mul_su). The divide chain alone sets Fmax, and it sits
behind the forward-unit mux and the operand mux. CoreMark (2K, -O3, rv32im) executes
almost no DIV/REM inside the timed bracket, so a long-latency divider costs almost no
iterations/cycle, while the clock period could drop several-fold. iterations/cycle
is ~unchanged, so fitness scales roughly with Fmax, and removing the divider chain
should clear the 4.6% acceptance threshold by a wide margin.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the divide a multi-cycle iterative unit that stalls the pipeline only when a
DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU is in EX, and share a single multiplier for MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU.

1. New module rtl/divider.sv (or logic inside ex_stage.sv): radix-2 restoring
   unsigned divider with sign pre/post-correction.
   - Registers: 32-bit remainder, 32-bit quotient/dividend shift reg, 32-bit abs(divisor),
     6-bit counter, flags q_neg, r_neg, want_rem, plus latched original a/b (RVFI-only
     consumers, pruned in the timed netlist).
   - State IDLE -> RUN (32 cycles, one shift/compare/subtract per cycle) -> DONE.
     In IDLE with a valid div op in EX and !stall_ex_mem, latch the forwarded
     post-mux rs1/rs2 (forwarding is correct in this first cycle only), take abs() for
     signed ops, set q_neg = signed & (a[31]^b[31]) & (b!=0), r_neg = signed & a[31].
     Division by zero needs no special mux: unsigned restoring division by 0 gives
     quotient all-ones and remainder = |a|; with q_neg forced to 0 when b==0 the DIV/DIVU
     result is 0xFFFFFFFF, and r_neg=a[31] restores REM = a. INT_MIN/-1 gives
     0x80000000 / 0 naturally.
   - `div_busy` = (div op in EX && valid && state != DONE). `div_busy` is high in the
     IDLE-start cycle and during RUN, low in DONE. In DONE the combinational result
     (sign-corrected quotient or remainder) is presented, EX/MEM captures it, state
     returns to IDLE. The FSM only advances when !stall_ex_mem (dmem stall freezes it).
   - In the DONE cycle, EX must report the *latched* a/b as rs1_val/rs2_val (RVFI), since
     the forward selects have changed after the bubbles went by.
2. rtl/ex_stage.sv: instantiate the divider; add a `div_busy` output. When div_busy is
   set and the EX/MEM register is not held by stall, EX/MEM captures a bubble ('0, so
   valid=0, rd=0, no reg_write, no mem op). Select the divider result for the four div
   ops through the existing alu result path (pass `div_res` into alu as a new input,
   or mux after the alu).
3. rtl/hazard_unit.sv + rtl/core.sv: take `div_busy`; stall_if |= div_busy,
   stall_id |= div_busy (ID/EX holds, same pattern as dmem_stall), and
   flush_id = (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall && !div_busy. A div in EX is never a
   branch/jump so `redirect` is 0 throughout. MEM/WB keeps retiring normally; bubbles
   do not bump rvfi_order.
4. rtl/alu.sv: add parameter COMB_DIV (default 1) so the existing combinational
   `/` `%` code remains the default for the cocotb alu unit test (test_alu.py is
   untouched and still checks exact RV32M bits). ex_stage instantiates alu with
   COMB_DIV=0, which removes the four divide/remainder cases and takes the divider result
   input instead. Keep the `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` branch unchanged and under ALTOPS
   tie div_busy to 0 so the formal flow still sees single-cycle div stand-ins.
5. Shared multiplier: replace mul_ss/mul_uu/mul_su with ONE signed 33x33 multiply:
   ax = {a[31] & signed_a, a}, bx = {b[31] & signed_b, b}, p = $signed(ax)*$signed(bx)
   where signed_a = (op is MULH or MULHSU), signed_b = (op is MULH). MUL/MULHU use
   the low/high halves of the same product. This cuts three 32x32 multipliers to one
   and reduces LUT/DSP usage and routing congestion in the ALU.
6. test/test_divider.py: new cocotb unit test driving the sequential divider with the same
   vectors as test_alu.py's div/rem cases (signed, unsigned, /0, INT_MIN/-1, negative
   dividends, plus a randomized sweep vs a Python reference), asserting 33-cycle latency
   and that the result is held in DONE.

Expected effect: the 200 ns divide path disappears; the next critical path is the
multiplier or the forward -> ALU -> EX/MEM chain, probably 40-70 ns, i.e. Fmax of
roughly 15-25 MHz versus 5.44 MHz. Div instructions are very rare in the timed CoreMark
region (core_list_join / matrix / state paths use shifts, multiplies, and compile-time
divides), so iterations/cycle moves by well under 1%. LUT4 should also fall by several
thousand. Correctness risks to check: the rs1_val/rs2_val RVFI fields in the DONE cycle,
the bubble not breaking forwarding of an older load (ID/EX holds while MEM/WB retires),
and a div that follows a load (existing load-use stall) or sits behind a dmem stall.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-001-r1s0 (regression, +681.60%): Swapping the combinational `/` `%` in alu.sv for a 33-cycle iterative divider took fitness ~7.8x (the 200 ns divide chain set Fmax and CoreMark issues almost no DIV/REM, so the stall costs ~nothing), but it still lost to sibling r1s1 (+749%), which also moved the multiplier into a multi-cycle MDU, so keeping even one shared single-cycle 33x33 multiplier in EX likely leaves the next Fmax limiter in place — take divide and multiply out of single-cycle EX together.

title: Move M-extension out of the EX ALU into a stalling multi-cycle MDU (iterative divider + 3-cycle DSP multiplier)
motivation:
The baseline closes timing at only 5.44 MHz (worst path 199.8 ns, 156 logic
cells, 150 logic levels) and the reported path is
mem_wb.rd -> forward_unit -> ex_stage fwd mux -> u_alu -> EX/MEM.alu_result.
The depth comes from alu.sv computing a fully unrolled combinational 32-bit
signed/unsigned `/` and `%` (plus a 32x32 -> 64 multiplier in three
sign variants) on every cycle, then muxing the result into the same 19-way
case as ADD/SLL/SLT. Every non-M instruction is therefore timed against the
divider's ripple of ~32 subtract-compare stages. CoreMark executes almost no
divisions (constants are strength-reduced at -O3) and only ~2-3K multiplies
per iteration out of ~449K cycles per iteration, so single-cycle M-ext
latency buys nothing measurable while it costs ~8x in Fmax. Fitness is
iter/cycle x Fmax; cycles are 4.49M for 10 iterations, so a >5x Fmax gain
dwarfs a ~1-2% cycle-count increase.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the M-extension into a separate sequential unit `rtl/mdu.sv`
that is NOT part of the single-cycle EX datapath, and make `alu.sv` base
RV32I only (ADD/SUB/AND/OR/XOR/SLT/SLTU/SLL/SRL/SRA/LUI). The core_pkg ALU_MUL..ALU_REMU
opcodes and the decoder stay unchanged; ex_stage routes them to the MDU.

MDU microarchitecture (all state is registered; only registers feed the
arithmetic, nothing combinational chains from the forwarding network into a
multiplier/divider):
  * Cycle 0 (M-op first reaches EX, MDU state IDLE): capture the
    forward-resolved rs1/rs2 (the `rs1`/`rs2` signals after the fwd muxes)
    and op into a_q/b_q/op_q. The operands MUST be captured this cycle
    because the MEM/WB / EX/MEM forwarding source disappears on the next
    cycle while ID/EX.rs?_val is stale.
  * Multiply (MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU): treat operands as 33-bit signed
    (sign-extend only when the op treats that operand as signed), split each
    into a 17-bit signed high part and 16-bit unsigned low part (zero-extended
    to 17 bits signed), so the four partial products a_l*b_l, a_l*b_h,
    a_h*b_l, a_h*b_h are 17x17 signed and map onto Gowin MULT18X18/DSP
    blocks. Cycle 1: register the four partial products. Cycle 2: sum
    pp_ll + ((pp_lh+pp_hl)<<16) + (pp_hh<<32), pick low/high word, assert
    `done` and present the result to the EX/MEM register. Total 3 cycles in
    EX = 2 extra stall cycles per multiply (~1% of CoreMark cycles). If the
    cycle-2 adder turns out to be the critical path in `make timing`, register
    the 64-bit sum and add one more cycle.
  * Divide/remainder: radix-2 restoring divider on |a| / |b| (unsigned
    magnitudes), 32 iterations of {shift remainder, 33-bit compare/subtract,
    set quotient bit}, one cycle each, followed by a sign-fix cycle
    (quotient negated iff signs differ and b!=0; remainder takes the
    dividend's sign). Special cases: b==0 -> DIV/DIVU quotient 0xFFFFFFFF and
    REM/REMU = a (force quotient to all-ones and skip negation when b==0);
    INT_MIN/-1 falls out correctly from the magnitude algorithm
    (|INT_MIN|=0x80000000, quotient negates back to 0x80000000, remainder 0).
    ~35 cycles per divide; irrelevant for CoreMark's op mix.
  * RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS: keep the same `ifdef` in mdu.sv. Under ALTOPS the
    MDU takes 2 cycles in EX (capture, then done) and the result is the same
    `(a+b)^const` / `(a-b)^const` formulas as today, computed on the captured
    a_q/b_q, so the formal gate still exercises the stall/bypass/retire
    plumbing. The non-ALTOPS branch implements the real arithmetic.

Pipeline integration (ex_stage + hazard_unit + core wiring):
  * `is_mdu = in.valid && in.ctrl.alu_op >= ALU_MUL` (M ops only come from
    the validated decoder arms; alu_op default is ALU_ADD). `mdu_stall =
    is_mdu && !mdu_done`; mdu_done is a pure function of the MDU state
    register (no dependence on fwd compare logic), so stall timing stays
    shallow.
  * hazard_unit gets a new `mdu_stall` input OR-ed into stall_if and stall_id
    (hold PC and ID/EX exactly like the load-use stall; flush_id is not
    asserted by mdu_stall; redirect can't fire while an M-op occupies EX).
  * While mdu_stall && !stall_ex_mem, the EX/MEM register captures a bubble
    (reg_q <= '0, valid=0, reg_write=0, no mem op) so the MEM and WB stages
    keep draining older instructions. dmem stall (stall_ex_mem) retains
    priority and simply freezes EX/MEM; the MDU holds its `done` state
    until EX/MEM accepts the result (state returns to IDLE only on
    done && !stall_ex_mem).
  * While the M-op sits in EX after cycle 0 (state != IDLE), the ex_stage's
    `rs1`/`rs2` operands used for EX/MEM.rs1_val/rs2_val/write_data (RVFI
    rs1_rdata/rs2_rdata) must come from the MDU's captured a_q/b_q, not the
    fwd muxes (their sources have drained by then). The mux select is the
    registered MDU state, so it adds one cheap level to the non-M operand path.
  * EX/MEM.alu_result for an M-op = MDU result in the `done` cycle; keep the
    existing `is_jump ? pc+4 : alu_result` mux and merge the MDU result in
    the same way (`is_mdu ? mdu_result : alu_result`, select = is_mdu from ID/EX
    register fields, not from the fwd network).

Expected result: the divider and 64-bit multiplier leave the single-cycle
timing graph entirely. What remains is fwd compare -> fwd mux -> alu_b mux ->
32-bit add/shift/slt -> result mux -> EX/MEM (~15 logic levels), the branch
compare -> redirect -> PC mux path, and the load-align path, putting Fmax in
the ~35-55 MHz range (6-10x baseline) at ~1-2% more cycles. Run `make
timing TARGET=bench` after implementation; if the next worst path is the MDU
multiplier sum, add a pipeline register there before touching anything else.
Area should drop too (a combinational 32-bit divider is thousands of LUT4s;
an iterative one is ~100 LUTs + ~100 FFs), staying under the 12.3K LUT
baseline.

title: IF-time predecode branch prediction (JAL always, bimodal BHT for conditionals)
motivation:
Every taken branch and every JAL/JALR currently resolves in EX, so the
wrong-path instruction fetched behind it is flushed (flush_if/flush_id on
`redirect`): one lost cycle per taken control transfer. The fetch stage has
no predictor at all (implicit predict-not-taken). In CoreMark roughly 10-15%
of retired instructions are taken branches or jumps, against a baseline CPI
of about 1.6-1.7 once the ~22% imem/dmem stalls are included, so the
redirect bubbles are a sizeable slice of the cycle count. Fmax is pinned at
~5.4 MHz by the combinational multiplier/divider path in the ALU (~200 ns),
far longer than any fetch-side path, so IPC gains from a predictor come at
no Fmax cost; a few extra LUTs/FFs in IF are free for the fitness metric.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Because imem data is returned combinationally in the same cycle as `pc`
(IF/ID is just a combinational bundle), the fetched instruction word can be
predecoded in IF itself. No BTB is needed: for JAL and conditional branches
the target is simply pc + imm computed from the instruction bits that
arrive in that same cycle. Proposal:

1. New module `bpred` (rtl/bpred.sv): a bimodal branch history table of
   2-bit saturating counters, 128 entries, indexed by pc[8:2]. Asynchronous
   read at fetch pc, synchronous write from EX. Counters reset to 2'b01
   (weakly not-taken); an un-reset LUT-RAM array is also acceptable since
   any initial predictor state is architecturally harmless.
2. In `if_stage`: predecode imem_data. JAL (opcode 1101111) is always
   predicted taken. A conditional branch (opcode 1100011 with
   funct3[2:1] != 2'b01, i.e. not the reserved funct3 = 2/3) is predicted
   taken iff its BHT counter is >= 2. Predicted target = pc + J/B-imm
   (small dedicated adder). Only predict taken when the instruction is
   valid (`!(flush||redirect)`, which already covers imem stall) AND the
   predicted target is word aligned (target[1:0] == 0), so the existing
   misaligned-target trap handling in EX is untouched. next_pc =
   redirect ? redirect_target : pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4. The PC
   register still holds on stall_if; the rule "instruction captured into
   ID/EX iff pc advanced this cycle" already holds for all stall/flush
   cases, so the prediction is always consumed consistently. Export
   `pred_taken` in the if_id_t bundle.
3. Carry `pred_taken` through id_stage into the ID/EX register (new field
   `pred_taken` in id_ex_t / if_id_t in core_pkg.sv; cleared on
   reset/flush like the rest of the register).
4. In `ex_stage` change redirect to be misprediction-driven:
     - conditional branch: mispredict = (branch_cond != in.pred_taken);
       redirect = mispredict && !misalign_fault;
       target = branch_cond ? branch_target : pc + 4.
     - JAL: redirect only if it was not predicted (pred_taken == 0; only
       happens with misaligned target, which traps and suppresses redirect
       anyway), so a predicted JAL costs zero bubbles.
     - JALR: unchanged (always redirect from EX, target = (rs1+imm)&~1).
   `reg_q.pc_next` (RVFI pc_wdata), alu_result (PC+4 link value),
   misalign trap logic and everything RVFI-visible are computed exactly as
   today, so rvfi_pc_wdata stays the architectural next PC regardless of
   prediction. Because redirect can be asserted repeatedly while EX is held
   by a dmem stall, the redirect target must be a pure function of the
   instruction in EX (it is) so repeats are idempotent.
5. BHT update in EX: when in.valid && in.ctrl.is_branch && !stall (the
   EX/MEM freeze), increment/decrement the counter at in.pc[8:2] with
   branch_cond. Gating on !stall prevents multi-update while EX is held.

Expected effect: JAL and well-predicted loop/branch back-edges drop from a
1-cycle bubble to zero; only mispredicts and JALR still pay one cycle.
Misprediction penalty is unchanged (1 cycle, same as a taken branch today),
so a mispredicted not-taken branch costs the same as it does now. Bimodal
accuracy on CoreMark's loop-dominated control flow is expected around 85-90%,
recovering most of the taken-branch/JAL bubbles (est. +6-10% IPC). Critical
path: the new logic is imem_data -> predecode -> 30-bit adder -> pc mux ->
PC reg and EX compare -> redirect -> pc mux; both are tens of ns, well under
the ~200 ns multiplier/divider path that sets Fmax, so Fmax is unchanged.
Correctness risk is low: prediction only changes which speculative path is
fetched; every wrong guess is squashed by the same flush mechanism used by
the baseline. Follow-up (not part of this hypothesis): return-address stack
for JALR.

changes.description: New module: 128-entry x 2-bit bimodal BHT, async read by fetch pc[8:2], synchronous counter update port driven from EX (pc, taken, enable).

title: Decouple EX redirect from IF/ID instr mux and ID/EX data-field reset
motivation:
After the MDU move the worst path is 27.3 ns / 41 cells / 21 logic levels and
its module trail is u_id -> u_ex -> u_if -> u_hazard -> u_id, ending on an
ID/EX register bit (id_ex_w.rs1_val_26) and starting at the regfile LUTRAM.
That is the branch-resolve loop: forwarded rs1/rs2 -> 32-bit compare ->
`redirect` -> (a) if_stage forces `out.instr` to NOP, which changes
rs1_addr/rs2_addr, so the late redirect re-addresses the regfile LUTRAM,
runs its x0/write-bypass compare and only then reaches ID/EX.rs?_val D
pins, and (b) hazard_unit's flush_id drives the synchronous reset of every
one of the ~230 ID/EX flops (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, instr, ...), a huge
fanout net on a part where routing dominates (0.66 ns/cell average).
Neither dependency is functionally required: flush_id already zeroes the
wrong-path instruction on a redirect, so the NOP mux on `redirect` is
redundant for ID/EX capture, and a bubble only needs `valid` and the
control bits cleared (data fields are don't-care when valid=0 and every
consumer is gated by ctrl.mem_read/mem_write/reg_write/is_branch/is_jump).
The score is Fmax x iterations/cycle and cycles do not change here, so
shortening the critical redirect loop converts directly into fitness.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two small, cycle-neutral edits that remove `redirect` from the two widest
fan-out cones it drives:

1. if_stage.sv: drop `redirect` from the IF/ID combinational payload.
   out.instr = imem_stall ? NOP : imem_data and out.valid = !imem_stall
   (flush input now carries only imem_stall; hazard_unit's flush_if becomes
   just `imem_stall`). On a redirect the wrong-path instruction in IF is
   never captured: with !dmem_stall, flush_id already resets the ID/EX
   control/valid bits; with dmem_stall, ID/EX is held (stall_id) and the
   redirect keeps being asserted by the branch still sitting in EX.
   PC priority (redirect > stall > pc+4) is unchanged, and a spurious
   load-use stall computed from the wrong-path instruction is harmless
   because redirect already overrides the PC and flush_id is asserted
   anyway. Result: redirect no longer feeds the regfile read address, the
   decoder, or the imm_gen; only flush_id -> ID/EX control reset and the
   PC mux depend on it.

2. id_stage.sv: split the ID/EX register into a control group and a data
   group. Control group (ctrl, valid) keeps `if (reset || flush) <= 0;
   else if (!stall) <= decoded`. Data group (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd,
   rs1_addr, rs2_addr, instr) becomes `if (reset) <= 0; else if (!stall)
   <= ...` -- no flush term, so flush_id fans out to ~25 flops instead of
   ~230 and the data flops' sync-reset pin is driven straight from the
   `reset` pin rather than from reset|flush logic. Bubbles therefore carry
   stale data with zeroed ctrl/valid: ctrl.is_branch/is_jump/mem_*/
   reg_write/alu_op(=ADD, <MUL) are all 0, so no redirect, no memory
   access, no regfile write, no MDU activation, no forwarding source
   (ex_mem_w_en=0) and no load-use hazard (id_ex_mem_read=0) can result.
   RVFI ignores fields when valid=0.

Pre-check: these exact edits (if_stage out.instr/out.valid use only
`flush`; hazard_unit flush_if = imem_stall; id_stage split into a
ctrl/valid always_ff with `reset || flush` and a data always_ff with
`reset` only) were applied to a scratch copy and run through
`make timing TARGET=bench`: place_option 0 went from 45.45 MHz (champion's
option 0) to 59.996 MHz (worst path 27.3 ns -> 21.96 ns, 14 logic levels,
LUT4 2397 vs 2433, FF 635 unchanged). The new worst paths are the
forwarding -> ALU -> dmem-address/EX-MEM cone, no longer the redirect loop.
Only one placement option was measured (the evaluator takes the median over
several), and cosim/formal were not run on the scratch copy; the edits are
cycle-neutral by construction, so CoreMark cycle count should remain
4,680,666 for 10 iterations. Do NOT add branch prediction or change CPI.
Re-run cosim + formal to confirm the retired instruction stream and CRCs.

title: Cut redirect out of the IF NOP-mux/load-use chain and narrow flush/bubble fan-out to control bits
motivation:
The MDU champion (48.2 MHz, 27.3 ns worst path, 41 cells) reports its worst
path through modules clock_ibuf > u_id > u_ex > u_if > u_hazard > u_id: the
ID/EX register -> forward muxes -> branch comparator -> `redirect` ->
if_stage's `(flush||redirect) ? NOP : imem_data` mux -> hazard_unit's
load-use 5-bit compares -> stall_id/flush_id -> clock-enable/sync-reset of
every ID/EX flop (~190 of them, so a very high-fanout net). Redirect is the
late EX signal, and it is currently pushed through *two* extra logic stages
and into a 190-flop control net, purely to NOP-out a wrong-path instruction
that the ID/EX flush already kills. IPC is fine (4.68M cycles); the
structure of the redirect/flush plumbing is what limits Fmax now.
`redirect` and `load_use_hazard` are mutually exclusive (redirect needs a
branch/jump in EX, load-use needs a load in EX), so the NOP mux on redirect
is not needed for hazard correctness either.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the squash plumbing so `redirect` reaches only the PC mux and a
handful of control flops, with no combinational path through the IF
instruction mux or the hazard compares:
1. if_stage / hazard_unit: drop `redirect` from the IF NOP substitution.
   `flush_if` becomes just `!imem_ready`; `out.instr = flush ? NOP : imem_data`,
   `out.valid = !flush`. PC priority (redirect over stall) is unchanged, so
   the redirect target is still always taken. The wrong-path instruction in
   IF during a redirect cycle is still captured into ID/EX but is squashed
   there (step 2). load_use is independent of redirect (a branch/jump in EX
   is never a load), so the compare no longer needs the masked instruction.
2. id_stage: split the ID/EX register into a flushable control part and an
   unflushed data part. On `flush` (redirect or load-use bubble) clear only
   what makes an entry a harmless bubble: `valid`, and ctrl.reg_write,
   mem_read, mem_write, is_branch, is_jump (plus is_illegal/alu_op may be
   left alone since everything is gated by valid / reg_write / mem_*).
   pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs*_addr, instr are cleared on `reset`
   only and otherwise follow the existing `!stall` enable. The flush net
   drops from ~190 sinks to ~12 and loses the redirect->stall_id CE path.
   Bubbles stay architecturally invisible: valid=0 keeps rvfi_valid, wb
   w_en and is_mdu low; reg_write=0 keeps the forward unit quiet; mem_read /
   mem_write=0 keep dmem_ren/wen and the hazard/dmem-stall logic quiet;
   is_branch/is_jump=0 keep redirect low.
3. ex_stage: the MDU-wait bubble (`mdu_stall`) currently clears the whole
   400-bit EX/MEM register; clear only `valid` and `ctrl` (reg_write /
   mem_read / mem_write live there) and leave payload bits unchanged, so
   the mdu_stall net fans out to ~25 flops instead of ~400. Data fields
   keep their sync reset on `reset`.
Behaviour and cycle counts are bit-identical to the champion (same
1-cycle taken-branch bubble, same load-use bubble, same stalls), so
CoreMark iter/cycle stays ~2.14e-6 and RVFI/formal are unaffected; the
gain is purely Fmax. The next critical path should become ID/EX ->
forward -> compare -> redirect -> PC mux, which is roughly 4-6 ns shorter
than the current 27.3 ns chain.

title: Fetch-time BHT/JAL/RAS prediction with registered mispredict recovery (EX redirect off the critical cone)
motivation:
On the current 48 MHz MDU core the reported worst path (27.3 ns, modules u_id > u_ex > u_if > u_hazard > u_id)
is the combinational EX redirect cone: id_ex regs -> forward mux -> 32-bit compare -> `redirect` -> if_stage
instruction NOP-gating (flush||redirect) -> hazard load_use / flush_id -> sync-reset/enable of the ~200 ID/EX flops
(and the PC mux). The previous predictor attempt (r1s2: JAL always + 128x2b BHT, still same-cycle redirect) cut
CoreMark cycles 6.4% (4.49M -> 4.20M) but was only tried on the 5 MHz core, and its LESSONS entry warns that a
same-cycle EX compare -> redirect -> next_pc path is no longer free on the 48 MHz core. Today every taken
branch/JAL/JALR costs a bubble (predict-not-taken), JALR returns are never predicted, and the redirect wire
is the Fmax limiter. A predictor whose recovery is *registered* attacks both factors of the fitness product at once.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small fetch-stage predictor and move mispredict recovery behind a flop:

1. New rtl/branch_predictor.sv (instantiated from if_stage), driven by the imem_data/pc already present in the
   combinational F/D cycle (imem_data is a flop output in the timed bench, so predecode is not input-delay limited):
     - predecode opcode of imem_data: JAL (always predict taken), BRANCH (taken if 2-bit counter MSB set), and
       `ret` (jalr x0, 0(x1): opcode 1100111, rd==0, rs1==1, imm==0) predicted from a 4-entry return-address stack.
       Calls (JAL/JALR with rd==x1) push pc+4. Push/pop ONLY when the fetch fires (imem_ready && !stall_if && !kill)
       so a re-presented held instruction does not double-push. No RAS repair on mispredict (perf-only pollution).
     - predicted target = pc + (J-imm or B-imm) via one dedicated 30-bit adder (pc[1:0]==0), or RAS top for ret.
       Do NOT predict taken if the static target has bit 1 set (misaligned) -> falls to existing trap semantics.
     - BHT: 128 x 2-bit saturating counters indexed by pc[8:2], written in EX; NO reset on the array so it infers
       LUT-RAM (predictor state is perf-only so uninitialised/zero-init is functionally safe, incl. formal).
       Read the counter at fetch and carry the 2-bit value in id_ex; EX writes back sat-inc/dec from the carried
       value (avoids a 2nd read port).
     - if_stage next_pc = kill ? redir_target_q : (pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4); out.valid = !(kill||imem_stall).
2. core_pkg id_ex_t gains pred_taken, pred_target[31:2] (needed for RAS check), bht_cnt[1:0]. id_stage latches them.
3. ex_stage: no combinational `redirect` any more. Compute mispredict = (is_branch && branch_cond != pred_taken)
   || (is_jump && !is_jalr && !pred_taken [only for the unpredicted misaligned/imm[1] case, which traps, so no redirect])
   || (is_jalr && !(pred_taken && rs1 == {pred_target,2'b00})). Correct-path target is selected by EARLY signals:
   is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],0} : (pred_taken ? pc+4 : pc+imm); on misalign_fault the instruction traps and (if the
   front end followed a predicted-taken path) the target is pc+4, else no redirect (keeps current trap behaviour).
   Register {redir_q, redir_target_q} only when the branch actually advances into EX/MEM (!stall_ex_mem && !mdu_stall
   && valid && !kill). While redir_q==1 (the next cycle) `kill` is high: the wrong-path instruction in EX is
   converted to a bubble (ex_mem <= '0; is_mdu/mdu `active` gated by !kill so a wrong-path MUL/DIV cannot start or
   stall), the instruction in F/D is dropped (flush_id includes kill), and PC <= redir_target_q (kill outranks stall_if).
   Mispredict penalty becomes 2 cycles (was 1), but correctly-predicted taken branches, all JALs and RAS-predicted
   returns cost 0 (were 1 each), and `redirect` no longer fans out combinationally from the 32-bit compare to PC mux,
   NOP-gating, hazard unit and ~200 ID/EX reset pins; the only late EX->control signal is a single D pin (redir_q).
4. hazard_unit: flush_id = (load_use || kill) && !dmem_stall; flush_if = kill || imem_stall; take load_use from the
   un-gated fetched instruction fields (kill is a flop so either is fine). if_stage no longer needs EX `redirect`.
5. The predicted-taken bit is latched into id_ex in the same cycle the PC advances to the predicted target (both use
   the same !stall_if cycle), so a held/stalled instruction is re-predicted consistently.

Expected cycle effect (from r1s2 data): ~-6% cycles from BHT+JAL, ~-2% from RAS-predicted returns, ~-2% given back
by the 2-cycle mispredict recovery -> roughly -5..-6% net cycles. The Fmax effect is the upside: removing the
EX compare -> redirect -> {PC, instr NOP-gate, load_use, flush_id} cone should let the next-longest paths (EX ALU
path, regfile read -> id_ex) set Fmax rather than the 27 ns redirect chain. Correctness is unaffected: wrong-path
instructions never become valid, rvfi_order/pc_next semantic is unchanged (pc_next still reflects the actual next PC).

title: Shorten the EX forward->ALU->EX/MEM cone: fold alu operand muxes into the forward mux, link/MDU result into the ALU result mux
motivation:
The champion (62.7 MHz, 0 IPC change since) is limited by one cone that every
recent attempt reports: ID/EX operand -> forward mux -> alu_a/alu_b source
mux -> ALU (adder + 11-way result mux) -> `alu_result | mdu` OR ->
`is_jump ? pc+4 : ex_result` mux -> EX/MEM.alu_result, which the timed
netlist absorbs as the dmem BSRAM address register (14 logic cells, ~22 ns).
Redirect/flush fan-out has already been removed from the critical set (r2s0,
r2s2); the remaining depth is plain datapath muxing in front of and behind
the adder. Three of those levels are pure plumbing, not arithmetic:
the alu_src/is_auipc 2:1 operand mux that sits after the 3:1 forward mux, the
OR that merges the MDU result, and the is_jump pc+4 mux after the ALU.

the alu_src/is_auipc 2:1 operand mux that sits after the 3:1 forward mux, the
OR that merges the MDU result, and the is_jump pc+4 mux after the ALU.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Remove those three mux levels from the EX cone without changing cycle count
or architectural behavior:
1. Operand muxes: replace `fwd 3:1 mux -> (alu_src ? imm : rs2)` with one 4:1
   mux per ALU operand whose select is a 2-bit code derived from
   {fwd_rs?_sel, alu_src / is_auipc}: A in {rs1_val, ex_mem, mem_wb, pc},
   B in {rs2_val, ex_mem, mem_wb, imm}. Forwarding is suppressed for an
   operand that is replaced by pc/imm (the forward compare result is simply
   overridden by the static ID/EX bit), so the data path is a single
   LUT4+MUX2_LUT5 level instead of two. The raw forwarded rs1/rs2 (needed
   for store data, branch compare, JALR sum, MDU capture, RVFI) keep their
   existing 3:1 muxes off the ALU path.
2. JAL/JALR link value: add ALU_LINK (5'd19) to core_pkg/decoder so jumps
   select `pc+4` inside the ALU's final case mux (pc+4 comes from a
   parallel 30-bit incrementer straight off ID/EX.pc) and delete the
   `is_jump ? pc+4 : ex_result` mux after the ALU in ex_stage. is_mdu must
   become a range check (ALU_MUL..ALU_REMU) so LINK is not seen as an M-op.
3. MDU merge: pass `mdu_result` into alu.sv as an input and select it in the
   case-mux (op in MUL..REMU) instead of `alu_result | (is_mdu ? mdu : 0)`.
   Result gating by valid/kill is unnecessary for the merge itself (a
   killed or invalid EX op is bubbled in EX/MEM); is_mdu stays gated for
   the stall/start handshake.
Everything else (forward_unit priority, hazard unit, branch predictor,
mdu.sv, RVFI plumbing) is untouched, so CoreMark cycles are identical
(4.43M) and the gain is pure Fmax from ~2-3 fewer levels in the
~14-level critical cone.

title: Resolve forwarding in ID: registered one-hot bypass selects and pre-muxed ALU operands
motivation:
The registered-kill core is limited by one cone: ID/EX flops ->
forward_unit compare (10-bit equality + w_en + x0 check + priority) -> 3:1
rs1/rs2 mux -> is_auipc / alu_src operand mux -> ALU (adder, shifter,
result case-mux) -> `is_jump ? pc+4 : ex_result` -> EX/MEM, with the branch
compare -> mispredict -> kill_q D and jalr_sum -> misalign -> ctrl.reg_write
cones hanging off the same forwarded operands (worst path 21.8 ns, 14 cells,
clock_ibuf > u_id > u_ex > u_alu > u_ex). Roughly 5 of those LUT levels sit
in front of the ALU and do nothing except decide *which* operand to use,
and that decision is fully known one cycle earlier, when the consumer is
still in ID. The design uses ~2.8k LUT4 and 832 FF, so spending a few dozen
extra flops to shorten the critical cone is cheap; the earlier lessons
(r2s0, r2s2) both found that Fmax, not CPI, is where the score moves.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move forwarding resolution out of EX and into ID, the classic "registered
bypass select" restructuring. It is cycle-neutral (no new stalls, the
forwarding network keeps the same two sources: EX/MEM.alu_result and the WB
data); only *when* the select is computed changes.

1. ID-stage select generation. While instruction I sits in ID (instruction
   bits from if_id.instr, the same source the regfile address and load-use
   check already use), compare I.rs1/I.rs2 with the rd of the instruction
   currently in EX (id_ex.rd, id_ex.ctrl.reg_write, rd != 0) and the one
   currently in MEM (ex_mem.rd, ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write, rd != 0). Whenever
   ID/EX captures I, the instruction in EX moves to EX/MEM and the one in
   MEM moves to MEM/WB, so these matches are exactly "forward from EX/MEM"
   (sel_ex) and "forward from MEM/WB" (sel_wb) next cycle. Capture and hold
   are tied together: stall_id (dmem stall, load-use, mdu stall) holds
   ID/EX, and the only stall in which EX/MEM shifts while ID/EX holds is the
   mdu stall, where the M-op samples its (already resolved) operands in its
   first EX cycle. kill/load-use flush writes zeros so the selects are 0.
   The select bits are added to id_ex_t as one-hot flags
   {a_ex,a_wb,b_ex,b_wb,s_ex,s_wb} and replace the combinational
   forward_unit compare in the EX cone.
2. Trap-cancel exactness. A producer's reg_write can still be cleared after
   the select was registered (misaligned JAL/JALR in EX, misaligned LOAD in
   MEM via ctrl_with_trap). So EX gates the registered selects with the
   producer's *registered* reg_write flop: use_ex = sel_ex & ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write,
   use_wb = sel_wb & mem_wb.ctrl.reg_write, priority use_ex > use_wb >
   ID/EX value. sel_wb is computed independently of sel_ex (not masked by
   it), so if a cancelled EX/MEM producer shadows a same-rd MEM/WB producer
   the older value is still found, and a cancelled producer with no older
   match falls through to the ID/EX value (the regfile read, which already
   includes any producer that was in WB at ID time via the write-first
   bypass). That keeps trap / reg-write suppression bit-exact with the
   current forward_unit, which also keys off ctrl.reg_write.
3. Pre-muxed ALU operands. In ID, capture op_a = is_auipc ? pc : rs1_data
   and op_b = alu_src ? imm : rs2_data into new ID/EX fields, with the
   a_*/b_* selects gated off when the operand is pc/imm (a_* &= !is_auipc,
   b_* &= !alu_src). The ALU then sees a_in = fwd(op_a), b_in = fwd(op_b)
   directly, deleting the is_auipc / alu_src mux level. rs1-side consumers
   other than the ALU (branch compare, jalr_sum, jalr_hit, MDU a) can use
   a_in, since none of them occur for AUIPC. The rs2-side consumers that
   must not see the immediate (branch compare, store write_data, MDU b)
   use a separately forwarded rs2 (s_ex/s_wb selects, ungated, from the raw
   rs2_val field). RVFI-only rs1_rdata/rs2_rdata keep using the existing
   combinational forward_unit + raw rs1_val/rs2_val so the RVFI contract and
   riscv-formal behavior are untouched; that logic only feeds RVFI and is
   pruned from the timed netlist. (If time is short, do steps 1, 2, 4 first
   and add step 3 afterwards; step 1 alone already removes the compare and
   priority levels.)
4. Fold the WB mux into MEM/WB. Capture wb_data = mem_to_reg ? load_data :
   alu_result in the MEM/WB register (retained across hold_wb like the other
   data fields) so wb_stage / regfile write data / the forward source is a
   plain flop output rather than flop -> mux; this removes a level from the
   MEM/WB -> EX bypass and the regfile write-data fan-out.

Expected effect: the EX cone loses ~3 levels of select logic (compare,
priority, and the 3:1 mux collapsing to a gated one-hot mux) plus one level
of operand mux, i.e. roughly 4-5 ns of ~16-21 ns, with every downstream
path (ALU -> EX/MEM, compare -> kill_q, jalr -> reg_write) starting later.
CoreMark iterations/cycle is unchanged (same stall/flush behavior, same
predictor), so the fitness gain is the Fmax gain. Risks: the ID-side
compare path starts at the imem_data input (same arrival as the existing
load-use compare, which is shallower than the regfile read -> ID/EX path),
and select flop fan-out (about 32 muxes each; duplicate the flops if
place-and-route shows them dominating). If the next limiter turns out to be
the ALU result case-mux or the compare chain, those are the follow-ups.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-002-r3s1 (improvement, +8.79%): Resolving forwarding in ID (one-hot `a_/b_/s_` ex/wb selects registered in ID/EX, gated in EX by the producers' registered `reg_write` so trap-cancelled JAL/JALR/LOAD stay bit-exact, plus pre-muxed `op_a`/`op_b` and a MEM/WB `wb_data` flop) was cycle-neutral and gained a real ~+9% Fmax, but only about half the +18% estimated from counting LUT levels removed, so deleting select/compare/operand-mux levels in front of the ALU is not enough on its own — the ALU adder/result case-mux, `is_jump ? pc+4` tail and branch-compare -> `kill_q` cone remain and are the next targets, and ID-side select compares/flop fan-out should be watched as new limiters.

title: Decouple the predicted fetch stream from backend stalls with a 4-entry instruction queue (bypassed when empty)
motivation:
Predictor accuracy is no longer the lever. I replayed the timed CoreMark window (2.92M retired
instructions between the 0x10000100/0x10000104 markers) through the Python ISS and a model of the
champion's predictor: 529,588 conditional branches, 54,452 bimodal-128 mispredicts (x2 cycles =
2.5% of the 4.43M cycles; a perfect predictor is the ceiling), 35,632 JAL + 13,735 call/ret pairs
(RAS-4 mispredicts: 12) and ZERO non-`ret` JALRs. Growing the BHT to 512 entries only cuts
mispredicts to 39,772 (~0.7% of cycles) and gshare is worse (42k-60k), so any BHT/BTB/gshare/JALR-cache
tweak is bounded by ~0.7% and would not clear the 4.6% acceptance bar.
The real front-end loss is stall *serialisation*. The bench injects ~22% imem stalls (fetch can
deliver at most 0.78 instr/cycle) and ~22% dmem stalls, and today the PC and the F/D instruction are
frozen by every backend stall (dmem_stall, load-use, MDU busy), so those cycles add to the imem
stalls instead of overlapping with them: the backend alone would sustain ~0.81 IPC and the fetch
~0.78 IPC, yet the measured IPC is 0.66 (4.43M cycles for 2.92M instrs).
A cycle-level model (random 78%-ready imem/dmem, load-use, MUL=3/DIV=35 cycles, 2-bubble registered
kill recovery, bimodal-128 mispredict flags from the real trace) reproduces the champion within 0.15%
(model 4,438,231 vs measured 4,431,994 cycles) and predicts, for a fetch queue between the
predicted-PC fetch stream and ID: 1 entry 4.34M, 2 entries 4.16M (-6.3% cycles), 4 entries 4.09M
(-7.8%), 8 entries 4.08M (-8.0%).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Turn the combinational F/D "stage" into a decoupled front end: the PC + branch_predictor keep
running ahead of the pipeline and push {pc, instr, pred_taken, pred_target, bht_cnt} into a small
instruction queue; ID pulls from the queue head. The predictor itself (predecode of the fresh
imem_data, JAL/BHT/RAS steering of the fetch PC, RAS push/pop at fetch) is unchanged.
1. if_stage.sv: add a 4-entry queue (shift-register organisation so the head is always entry 0, or a
   circular buffer with a registered one-hot head -- implementer's choice; ~95 bits/entry, flops, no
   reset except the occupancy counter). Fetch consumes a slot when `fire = imem_ready && !full && !kill`
   where `full` comes from the occupancy flops only (occupancy before this cycle's pull -- this is the
   conservative behaviour the model assumed). pc <= kill ? kill_target : (fire ? next_pc : pc). The
   RAS push/pop and BHT read use `fire` exactly as today (each instruction is predicted/pushed once).
   Decode source: head = queue_empty ? {pc, imem_data, pred...} (bypass, valid = imem_ready) : queue[0]
   (valid = 1). The bypass keeps the fetch->EX latency and the 2-bubble mispredict penalty of today's
   design. An instruction is enqueued iff fire && !(queue_empty && pull); dequeued iff pull &&
   !queue_empty. On kill the queue is flushed (occupancy <= 0) and no fetch fires, matching the
   existing registered-recovery behaviour (kill outranks stall; kill_q held through a dmem stall).
2. hazard_unit.sv: stall_if disappears as a PC-enable (the PC no longer waits for dmem/MDU/load-use).
   load_use is computed from the head instruction's rs1/rs2 fields (instead of raw imem_data) against
   ID/EX. Add `pull = head_valid && !dmem_stall && !mdu_stall && !load_use && !kill`; stall_id (ID/EX
   holds) = dmem_stall || mdu_stall (as today); flush_id (bubble) = (load_use || kill || !head_valid)
   && !dmem_stall; out.valid = head_valid && !kill. stall_ex_mem / hold_mem_wb / mdu handshakes are
   untouched.
3. core.sv / id_stage.sv: wire `pull`/head_valid between hazard_unit and if_stage and feed
   if_id_t.valid from head_valid; ID/EX capture is otherwise unchanged. ex_stage and
   branch_predictor are untouched (kill/kill_target, BHT update, MDU gating stay as in the champion).
Expected: -6% to -8% cycles at unchanged Fmax (model: Q=2 -6.3%, Q=4 -7.8%). Timing notes: the PC
enable no longer depends on the hazard/MDU/dmem-stall cone (only on imem_ready and an occupancy flop),
which removes a fan-in from the PC mux; the new logic is one 2:1 bypass mux ahead of decode/regfile
read (the ID path is not the reported critical path -- that is the forwarding -> ALU -> EX/MEM cone)
and a pull-enable fanned out to the queue flops. If the bypass mux or pull fan-out costs Fmax,
fall back to 2 entries (still -6.3% cycles in the model). Cost ~400 FF / ~300 LUT of the 20K budget.

title: Flatten ALU/link/MDU result select to one-hot AND-OR and drop address-reg gating
motivation:
Cycles are already ~4.43M, essentially at the 22% imem-stall fetch bound, so
only Fmax matters. I ran `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion: the 25
worst paths all run regfile-BRAM DO (2.26 ns tC2Q) -> op_a LUT -> 2-LUT
forward mux (a_in) -> a 3-cell adder carry (SUM at ~12.8 ns) -> SIX serial
1-fanout LUTs (u_ex/n1318_s22,s18,s11,s5,s3,s2: the alu `case` priority
chain, the MDU OR and the `is_jump ? pc+4 : ex_result` mux) -> a fanout-4
LUT (dmem_addr_c_b_b_b_2, the reset/hold gating that Gowin leaves in front
of the BRAM address register it absorbed) -> dmem BRAM ADB. After the adder
result is known (12.85 ns) the path still burns 7.6 ns (20.42 arrival),
half of it in that 6-level mux chain and the address gating. The adder
itself is only 3 cells deep here, so the select logic, not the arithmetic,
is the limiter.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild the post-arithmetic select as a flat, balanced AND-OR whose
selects are decoded from registered state in parallel with the operand
forward muxes (so they cost no path depth), instead of a serial priority
chain. (1) alu.sv (ports/op encodings unchanged, so test_alu.py and

or, xor, slt, sltu, sll, srl, sra, lui) in a separate always_comb that

title: Dedicated AGU + separate memory-address register, control/data split of EX/MEM
motivation:
Every recent champion/runner-up reports the same worst path class:
ID/EX -> forward mux -> ALU (shifter / adder / 11-way result case mux) ->
`is_jump ? pc+4` tail -> MDU OR -> reset/hold/bubble mux -> EX/MEM.alu_result,
and the endpoint in the Gowin report is always a dmem BSRAM (`dmem_N_dmem_N_0_0_s`),
because the dmem read is `dmem[dmem_addr[12:2]]` and synthesis absorbs the
EX/MEM.alu_result flops into the BSRAM address registers. So the ALU result
cone (13-14 LUT levels) also has to reach four BSRAM address pins across the
die, with the sync-reset / bubble / stall muxes folded in front of them, while
the same flops fan out to three forwarding muxes. The load/store address is
just a_in + imm; it does not need the ALU result mux, the JAL/JALR link mux or
the MDU merge at all. Separately, r2s0 showed that removing bubble/flush clearing
from ID/EX *data* flops (clearing only ctrl/valid) gave a real +32% Fmax because
the high-fan-out control net (here `kill_q | mdu_stall | stall | reset`, derived
from the late `is_mdu`/`mdu_done` logic) was the limiter, not logic depth. EX/MEM
still clears ~300 data flops on that same net.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Structural change in three coordinated parts, all cycle-neutral (no change to
pipeline depth, forwarding, hazards, or prediction):

1. Add a dedicated address-generation adder in ex_stage:
   `agu_sum = a_in + in.imm` (a_in is the forwarded rs1 for every LOAD/STORE since
   alu_src=1 and is_auipc=0; identical to what the ALU computes with ALU_ADD, so
   RVFI mem_addr / misalign traps stay bit-exact). It feeds a NEW EX/MEM field
   `mem_addr` (added to ex_mem_t in core_pkg.sv) that is a plain flop with only a
   clock-enable (!stall) - no reset, no bubble clear, no result mux in front. The
   path to the BSRAM address becomes: ID/EX flop -> forward mux -> 32-bit carry
   chain -> flop/BSRAM address register, i.e. ~4-5 levels instead of 13-14.
2. mem_stage uses `in.mem_addr` instead of `in.alu_result` for dmem_addr, byte_mask,
   mem_misalign and the RVFI aligned_addr. `alu_result` stays only for ALU/JAL/JALR/
   MDU results (forwarding to EX and the `wb_data` mux), so those flops are now
   ordinary logic flops that placement can put next to the ALU/forward muxes
   instead of being pulled toward the BSRAM columns. dmem_wdata/WEn/REn remain
   flop -> small decode, unchanged.
3. Split the EX/MEM register into a control block and a data block. Only `ctrl`
   and `valid` keep the `reset / stall-hold / (mdu_stall||kill_q) -> 0` behaviour.
   Data fields (pc, alu_result, write_data, rd, rs1_addr, rs2_addr, rs1_val,
   rs2_val, pc_next, branch_*, instr, mem_addr) become `if (!stall) q <= d` with no
   reset and no bubble clearing: every consumer is already gated by the registered
   ctrl.reg_write / mem_read / mem_write / valid (ex_rw gating in forwarding,
   forward_unit's ex_mem_w_en, hazard_unit's ex_mem_mem_op, rd_wen and
   aligned_addr gating in mem_stage/core), and MEM/WB already carries stale data
   with valid=0 on hold_wb, so formal/cosim see nothing new. This removes the
   late is_mdu/mdu_stall/kill_q signal from the SR/CE nets of ~300 flops and maps
   the hold onto the dedicated CE pin.

the budget (2953 of 10000 LUT4). IPC is unchanged. Expected effect is a worst path
that ends at an ordinary flop with 2-4 fewer levels and a lighter control fan-out,
worth roughly +6..10% Fmax; the next limiter will be forward mux -> shifter/adder ->
result mux -> alu_result flop and the branch-compare -> kill_q cone.

only `mem_addr` on bubble/reset (it is a single 32-bit field).

title: Run the predicted fetch stream ahead of backend stalls with a 3-entry fetch queue (flop-only control, PC enable off the dmem/MDU/load-use stalls)
motivation:
The champion's predictor is already near its ceiling. From r3s2's trace replay: 529,588 conditional
branches in the timed window, 54,452 bimodal-128 mispredicts (about 3 cycles each with the registered
`kill` recovery = ~3.7% of the 4.43M cycles even if the predictor were perfect), 12 RAS-4
mispredicts, and no non-`ret` JALRs. A 512-entry BHT recovers only ~1%, and gshare is worse, so
BHT/BTB/gshare tweaks cannot clear the 4.6% acceptance bar. The remaining front-end loss is
serialisation of stalls: the PC and the F/D instruction freeze on every dmem stall, load-use bubble
and MDU busy cycle. The ~22% random imem stalls are then paid again on top of them, because the
instruction that was fetched during a backend stall is thrown away and has to be re-fetched
(78% ready) after the stall ends. Measured IPC is 0.66 (4.43M cycles / 2.92M instructions) while
fetch alone could deliver 0.78 and the backend alone about 0.81.
r3s2 already proved the cycle side on the old 62.7 MHz base. A 4-entry queue gave exactly the
modelled 4,086,099 cycles (-7.8%), but the extra 390 flops and the 18-cell critical cone cost
~5% Fmax (59.5 vs 62.7), so the net was only +2.8% and it lost the 4.6% bar. The cycle gain is a
sure thing. This hypothesis redoes the idea with explicit Fmax-protection rules so that less of the
gain is given back on the new 68.3 MHz base.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Turn the combinational F/D point into a decoupled, predictor-fed fetch queue, written so the queue
adds almost nothing to the EX -> dmem-address cone that sets Fmax.

1. Queue: a 3-entry shift-register FIFO in if_stage.sv (head always at entry 0), entries
   {pc[31:2], instr, pred_taken, pred_target[31:2], bht_cnt[1:0]}. The branch_predictor module is
   unchanged. It still predecodes the fresh imem_data, steers the fetch PC and does RAS push/pop and
   the BHT read, and every instruction is fetched, predicted and pushed exactly once.
   `fire = imem_ready && !full && !kill`, where `full` and `empty` come ONLY from registered
   occupancy state (a one-hot or thermometer occupancy register, no adders). pc <= kill ? kill_target
   : fire ? next_pc : pc. The PC enable no longer contains dmem_stall, load_use or mdu_stall, which
   removes the late dmem_ready/MDU-done inputs from the PC / imem-address register enable.
2. Decode source: head = empty ? {pc, imem_data, pred_*, valid = imem_ready && !kill} : queue[0]
   (valid = !kill). The empty-queue bypass keeps the fetch-to-EX latency and the registered-kill
   mispredict penalty of the champion. The instruction word is a single 2:1 mux level in front of ID.
   An instruction is enqueued iff fire && !(empty && pull). It is dequeued iff pull && !empty. On
   `kill` the queue is flushed (occupancy <= 0), no fetch fires, and kill_q stays held through a dmem
   stall exactly as today.
3. hazard_unit.sv: load_use is computed on the HEAD instruction's rs1/rs2 (head = bypass or
   queue[0]) against ID/EX. `pull = head_valid && !dmem_stall && !mdu_stall && !load_use && !kill`.
   stall_id = dmem_stall || mdu_stall (ID/EX holds, as today). flush_id = (load_use || kill ||
   !head_valid) && !dmem_stall (bubble). stall_if / flush_if are replaced by pull/head_valid. The
   regfile read addresses and forward_unit select generation must use the head instruction, not raw
   io_imemData. core.sv rewires if_id_rs1/rs2 and the id_stage `in` bundle to the head.
4. Fmax protection rules:
   (a) no queue or occupancy signal may reach ex_stage, mem_stage or the forwarding / ALU cone. The
       only coupling is `pull`, which feeds the ID/EX hold/bubble controls that already exist;
   (b) keep the ID/EX sync-reset/enable fan-out as today: control bits flush/hold, data flops
       enable only;
   (c) queue data flops have no reset (only the occupancy register resets) and carry enables, not
       resets;
   (d) the queue stores pred_target only because `ret` needs it for the EX RAS check. Optional area
       trim: derive entry pcs from the preceding entry's pred_target / pc+4 instead of storing 30-bit
       pcs per entry.
5. Optional free predictor tweak if area allows: grow the BHT from 128 to 256 entries (pc[9:2]
   index, LUT-RAM, no reset). The trace showed ~1% fewer mispredict cycles at 512 entries.

Expected cycle effect from the r3s2 model, which matched its measurement exactly: 2 entries -6.3%,
4 entries -7.8%, so 3 entries is about -7% (~4.12M cycles). If Fmax stays within ~2.5% of 68.3 MHz,
fitness lands at about 161-166, above the 4.6% bar. The smaller queue (3 vs 4 entries, ~280 vs ~390
flops) and the shorter PC-enable cone are meant to avoid r3s2's Fmax loss.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-003-r4s2 (regression, +6.12%): A 3-entry decoupled fetch queue (PC enable freed from dmem/MDU/load-use stalls, empty-queue bypass, registered occupancy, reset-free queue data flops, only `pull` touching the ID/EX hold/bubble controls) beat the 4-entry r3s2 version of the same idea (+2.84%, Fmax 59.5 MHz) and, since fitness is ~Fmax/cycles, apparently kept most of the ~7% cycle gain with Fmax near the 68 MHz base, so keeping queue/occupancy state out of the EX -> dmem-address cone is what makes front-end decoupling pay, but it still ranked a regression behind the Fmax-only sibling r4s1 (+11.95%, 76.4 MHz) — the CPI lever (CoreMark is already at the ~22% imem-stall fetch bound without it) is worth re-trying only on top of the fastest EX/MEM base, where the extra ~300 flops and `pull` fan-out will have to fit a ~13 ns cone.

title: Build the regfile from fabric flops so EX operands launch from real flops, not BSRAM DO
motivation:
`make timing` on the current champion (Fmax 75.3 MHz, 13.24 ns data path) shows
that the top paths (path 1..5 and the rest of the list) ALL start at the
same cell, `cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s`, a Gowin BSRAM (BSRAM_R28, CLKB -> DO[4]).
Gowin synthesis turned the 32x32 async-read register file plus the ID/EX operand
flops behind it into a sync-read BSRAM: the ID/EX operand register has been
absorbed into the RAM, so in the EX cycle op_a / op_b / rs2 are launched by
the BSRAM output with tC2Q = 2.260 ns (a fabric flop is ~0.5 ns), followed by
the bypass/op-select LUT (u_id `op_a_N_s16`) and then the forward mux
LUTs (`a_in_N_s1`, `a_in_N_s0`), the 32-bit carry chain, and the
compare / result logic. Concretely path 1 is:
BSRAM DO (2.26) -> op_a LUT (0.97) -> a_in LUT (1.14) -> a_in LUT (1.20)
-> carry chain (~2.4 incl. entry route) -> 3 LUTs + routes -> upd_taken_q.
The same 2.26 ns + 3 LUT prefix starts every alu_result_N and kill_q path, so
it is common-mode to the whole critical group: shaving later logic one path
at a time (r3/r4 work) cannot move all of them, but replacing the launch
element can. LESSONS say prior wins came from decoupling late/awkward
endpoints (BSRAM address pins, SR/CE fan-out); this is the same effect at
the other end of the cone (a BSRAM *startpoint*).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make reg_file.sv a flop-based register file so Gowin cannot infer a BSRAM for
it, and the ID/EX operand registers stay ordinary fabric flops placed next to
the EX forward muxes:

- Store the registers as 31 explicit 32-bit flop vectors (x0 is not stored),
  not as an unpacked `regs[0:31]` memory. Preferred form that does not get
  recognized as a RAM: a packed `logic [32*32-1:0]` (or a generate loop over
  32 named `logic [31:0] r` regs) with a one-hot per-register write enable
  decoded from w_addr (`we[i] = w_en && w_addr == i`), write via
  `if (we[i]) r[i] <= w_data` in the generate block, and the two read ports as
  `rf[rs1_addr*32 +: 32]` / `rf[rs2_addr*32 +: 32]` (mux tree). Optionally add the
  Gowin attribute `(* syn_ramstyle = "registers" *)` as well, but do not rely on
  it alone: check that the netlist report shows no `u_rf/regs_*` BSRAM.
- Keep exactly the same behaviour: x0 reads as 0, write-first bypass
  (`w_en && w_addr == rs_addr` returns w_data), synchronous reset clearing all
  registers (flops make this free; no LUT cost), no port changes. id_stage's
  ID/EX register, forwarding, and hazard logic are untouched.
- Timing consequence: the ID-side read path becomes imem BSRAM DO (2.26 ns,
  from the instruction fetch) -> 32:1 mux tree (3 LUT levels) -> bypass mux ->
  op_a/op_b mux -> ID/EX flop, about 8-9 ns, well under the 13 ns EX budget.
  The EX-side launch point becomes an ordinary flop with ~0.5 ns clk->Q and
  local routing instead of a 2.26 ns BSRAM output, removing about 1.7 ns
  (~13%) from every path in the current critical group. Cycle count is
  identical (the regfile is read in ID and registered into ID/EX in both
  forms), so fitness moves with Fmax only.
- Cost: +~1100 flops and ~600-700 LUT4 for the two 32:1 read mux trees
  (core is at 2993/10000 LUT4, 898 FF), one fewer BSRAM pair. Watch that the
  new limiter is the imem-DO -> mux tree -> ID/EX path and the forward mux /
  carry-chain cone in EX; if the read mux tree becomes critical, register
  nothing extra but split the read mux by rs[4] with a late 2:1.

title: Control/data plane split of ID/EX and MEM/WB plus one shared branch comparator
motivation:
The r4s1 champion (76.4 MHz) got +12% from splitting EX/MEM into a small
reset/bubble-controlled control plane (ctrl, valid) and a large data plane
that only has a clock enable. The same trick was never applied to the other
two big registers in this lineage. id_stage.sv still does
`if (reset || flush) reg_q <= '0; else if (!stall) ...` on the whole ~330-flop
ID/EX struct, so `flush_id = (load_use_hazard || kill) && !dmem_stall` (which
starts from the LFSR/imem instruction bits, a compare against id_ex_rd, and
the dmem_ready stall term) and `reset` drive the sync-reset pins of every
data flop, and `stall_id` drives their clock enables: three late,
~250-fanout nets whose routing alone costs 2-3 ns. mem_stage.sv likewise
resets the entire ~340-flop MEM/WB struct on `reset`. The earlier r2s0
experiment (data flops of ID/EX with no flush clear) was worth +32% Fmax on
the 48 MHz core, but r2s0 lost to a sibling and is not in the champion's
lineage, so this is still unclaimed Fmax. Separately, the current worst
path in the log (regfile/ID-EX operand -> forward mux -> branch compare ->
`upd_taken_q`, 35 cells) ends on the branch comparator, which instantiates
signed and unsigned magnitude compares plus an equality compare, all hanging
off the heavily loaded a_in / s_in nets.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three coordinated structural edits, all cycle-neutral (no change to pipeline
depth, hazards, prediction, forwarding or retirement order):

1. ID/EX control/data split (rtl/id_stage.sv). Only `ctrl` and `valid` keep
   `if (reset || flush) <= '0`. Every other field (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm,
   rd, rs1_addr, rs2_addr, instr, pred_*, bht_cnt, op_a, op_b and the
   a_*/b_*/s_* bypass flags) moves to a second always_ff with only
   `if (!stall) q <= d`: no reset, no flush clear, so the flush/reset nets
   fan out to ~30 flops and stall_id maps onto the CE pins. Bubble safety:
   a bubble has ctrl == 0 and valid == 0, and every consumer of the data
   plane is already gated by registered ctrl/valid (reg_write in
   forward_unit/ex_stage ex_rw, is_branch/is_jump/is_jalr for mispredict and
   bht_upd_valid, mem_read/mem_write in hazard_unit and mem_stage, in.valid
   for is_mdu), exactly the argument r4s1 used for EX/MEM. Stale
   a_*/b_*/s_* flags on a bubble only select between data that is ignored.
2. MEM/WB control/data split (rtl/mem_stage.sv). `reset` clears only `valid`
   and `ctrl` (reg_write must be 0 so wb_stage/forwarding see no write);
   hold_wb already clears only `valid`. All data fields (pc, wb_data, rd,
   rs*_addr/val, pc_next, mem_*, instr) become reset-free `else` flops. They
   are consumed only under ctrl.reg_write && valid (regfile write, EX
   forwarding via ex_stage's mem_wb_reg_write gate) or by RVFI.
3. One shared branch comparator (rtl/ex_stage.sv). Replace the six-way case
   of ==, !=, signed <, signed >=, unsigned <, unsigned >= (three separate
   carry chains/compare trees) with one equality compare and one unsigned
   magnitude compare on operands whose MSBs are XORed with
   `!in.ctrl.branch_op[1]` (funct3 4/5 are signed, 6/7 unsigned; the bit is
   already a registered ID/EX flop, so no new field or ctrl_t change is
   needed). Then branch_cond = branch_op[2] ? (lt ^ branch_op[0])
                                             : (eq ^ branch_op[0]).
   This removes one 32-bit chain and its fan-out from a_in/s_in and leaves
   two LUT levels after the compare in front of kill_q / upd_taken_q. Also
   clear reg_write on a misaligned fault only for `misalign_jump` (a branch
   never has reg_write set, so behaviour is identical; is_illegal may still
   use misalign_fault since it feeds only RVFI), which takes the compare
   result out of the ctrl.reg_write flop's D cone.

Cost: no new state; LUT count should drop slightly (one fewer comparator,
fewer reset muxes). Expected effect: lighter late control nets and a
shorter branch-compare cone, roughly +4..9% Fmax with unchanged
iterations/cycle. Keep alu.sv, the ALU localparams, the decoder port list
and ctrl_t untouched (test_alu.py / _helpers.py mirror them). If formal
objects to uninitialised data flops on bubbles, fall back to also clearing
only `instr`/`rd`/`rs*_addr` on flush (small fields).

implementation_notes:
# Implementation notes: control/data split of ID/EX and MEM/WB (+ shared-comparator experiment)

## What shipped (all under cores/bench/rtl/)

1. `id_stage.sv` — ID/EX register split in two `always_ff` blocks.
   - Control block: only `ctrl` and `valid` keep `if (reset || flush) <= '0; else if (!stall) <= d`.
   - Data block: every other field (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs1_addr,
     rs2_addr, instr, pred_taken, pred_target, bht_cnt, op_a, op_b,
     a_ex/a_wb/b_ex/b_wb/s_ex/s_wb) is `if (!stall) q <= d` — no reset, no
     flush clear. `reset`/`flush` fan out to ~30 flops and `stall_id`
     maps to clock-enable pins.
2. `mem_stage.sv` — MEM/WB register split.
   - Control block: `reset` clears `ctrl` and `valid`; `hold_wb` clears only
     `valid` (unchanged); otherwise `ctrl <= ctrl_with_trap`, `valid <= in.valid`.
   - Data block: all data fields (pc, wb_data, rd, rs*_addr/val, pc_next,
     mem_addr/rdata/wdata/wmask/rmask, instr) written with `if (!hold_wb)`,
     no reset.
3. `ex_stage.sv` — misaligned trap: `reg_write` is cleared only for
   `misalign_jump` (a branch never has reg_write set); `is_illegal` is still
   set on `misalign_fault`. This takes the compare result out of the
   `ctrl.reg_write` flop's D cone.

alu.sv, decoder ports, ctrl_t, core_pkg localparams, test files: untouched.

## Deviation: the shared branch comparator was NOT kept

I implemented edit 3 exactly as proposed (one `==` plus one unsigned `<` on
operands with the MSB XORed with `!branch_op[1]`, `branch_cond =
branch_op[2] ? lt ^ op[0] : eq ^ op[0]`), verified it (formal 53/53, cosim
pass), then measured it with the Gowin flow (`python3 -m tools.eval.gowin bench
--all-options`, median of 3 placement options):

| variant                                              | p0     | p1     | p2     | median |
|------------------------------------------------------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| baseline (HEAD) place-option 0 only                  | 75.3   |   -    |   -    | (core.yaml champion: 76.4) |
| all three edits (shared comparator)                  | 62.4   | 70.6   | 70.6   | 70.6   |
| shared comparator only (ID/EX, MEM/WB unsplit)       | 71.5   | 71.1   | 71.1   | 71.1   |
| ID/EX + MEM/WB split only (baseline ex_stage)        | 72.9   | 75.2   | 75.2   | 75.2   |
| **shipped**: splits + jump-only reg_write clear      | 74.7   | 75.1   | 75.1   | 75.1   |

The shared comparator made Fmax worse (71.1 vs 75.2): the MSB XOR adds a LUT
level in front of the compare carry chain on a_in/s_in (a_in is a fan-out-15
net), which outweighs the saved comparator, and the branch-compare cone was
never the sole limiter anyway: in the baseline report path 1 (compare ->
`upd_taken_q`, 35 cells) and path 2 (BSRAM regfile DO -> op_a LUT -> 2-LUT
forward mux -> ALU carry -> 6-7 serial LUT result-select chain ->
`alu_result`) are both 18.57 ns. After the splits the ALU result-select chain
is the limiter regardless of the compare, so speeding up the compare cannot
help. The shipped design therefore keeps the original six-way compare `case`.

The control/data splits themselves were Fmax-neutral on this base (75.2 vs the
75.3 baseline p0 / 76.4 champion median: within placement noise, 1 MHz), with
~60 fewer LUTs (2931 vs 2993) and unchanged cycles. The flush/reset/stall
nets of ID/EX were evidently not the limiter once the EX/MEM split (r4s1)
and the registered kill were in place; the remaining limiter is the
BSRAM -> forward mux -> ALU -> result-select -> EX/MEM.alu_result cone.

Expected effect: ~neutral Fmax, slightly smaller area, identical IPC.

## Bubble-safety argument

A bubble in ID/EX has ctrl == 0, valid == 0. Every consumer of the ID/EX data
plane is gated by registered ctrl/valid: forward_unit uses `id_ex_rd` only
with `id_ex_w_en` (ctrl.reg_write); hazard_unit uses `id_ex_rd` only with
`mem_read`; EX uses is_branch/is_jump/is_jalr (misalign, mispredict,
bht_upd_valid), `in.valid` (kill recovery, bht update, is_mdu). The stale
a_*/b_*/s_* flags only steer data that goes nowhere: the EX/MEM and MEM/WB
control planes are zero/valid=0 for that slot. Same argument for MEM/WB: data
is read only under ctrl.reg_write (+valid for the regfile write) or by RVFI
under valid. During a load-use stall the ID/EX control block takes the bubble
(flush wins over stall) while the data block holds (stall_id = 1); harmless as
above.

## Verification (final shipped RTL)

- `verilator --lint-only -Wall -Wno-MULTITOP -sv +incdir+cores/bench/rtl cores/bench/rtl/*.sv`: clean.
- Cosim (`NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench`): passed, 2 ELFs (selftest + CoreMark
  CRCs). (`make cosim` without `NRET=1` builds with -DNRET=2 and fails to
  compile main.cpp against this nret=1 core; that is a Makefile default, not
  an RTL issue.)
- Formal: `RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench bash formal/run_all.sh`
  (no config argument, so nret=1 is auto-detected -> wrapper_si.sv +
  checks_si.cfg). The full-hypothesis variant passed 53/53; the final shipped
  variant: see the line at the bottom of this file. (Passing
  `formal/checks_si.cfg` explicitly disables the auto-detection and selects
  the dual-channel wrapper, which fails on an nret=1 core regardless of RTL.)

## Concerns

- Data flops of ID/EX / MEM/WB are uninitialised until the first non-stalled
  cycle after reset; all consumers are gated by ctrl/valid, so there is no
  observable effect (formal and cosim agree).
- The Fmax measurements above are single runs of a noisy placer; differences
  under ~1.5 MHz should not be read as signal.

## Final local status

Final shipped RTL: lint clean, formal 53 passed / 0 failed (nret=1 wrapper), cosim passed (2 ELFs).
lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-002-r5s1 (regression, -1.72%): Extending the r4s1 "reset/bubble only on ctrl+valid" split to ID/EX and MEM/WB was Fmax-neutral (75.2 vs 75.3 MHz, ~60 fewer LUTs) because once EX/MEM was split and `kill_q` registered the flush/stall nets were no longer the limiter, and the shared signed/unsigned branch comparator (MSB XOR with `!branch_op[1]` into one `<`) cost ~4 MHz (71.1) since the XOR adds a LUT level ahead of the carry chain on the fan-out-15 `a_in`, so keep the six-way compare `case` and treat reset/CE-pin trimming as exhausted — compare->`upd_taken_q` and regfile-DO->forward mux->ALU->result-select->`alu_result` were tied at 18.57 ns, so any further Fmax gain has to shorten the ALU result-select/regfile-launch cone, not one of the two paths alone.

title: Predictor-fed 2-entry fetch queue on the 76 MHz EX/MEM base (PC enable off backend stalls)
motivation:
Direction-prediction accuracy is no longer a lever. I replayed the timed CoreMark window (2.92M
retired instructions between the 0x10000100/0x10000104 markers) through the Python ISS and a model
of the champion's predictor: 529,588 conditional branches, ~50k bimodal-128 mispredicts (x2 cycles
~= 100k of the ~4.43M cycles = 2.3%, and that is the ceiling for a perfect predictor), 12 RAS-4
mispredicts and ZERO non-`ret` JALRs (so a JALR/BTB cache has nothing to predict). Any BHT size /
gshare / BTB change is therefore bounded well below the 4.6% acceptance bar.
The remaining front-end loss is stall *serialisation*: the PC and the combinational F/D instruction
freeze on every dmem stall, load-use bubble and MDU-busy cycle, so the ~22% random imem stalls are
paid again on top of them (the instruction fetched during a backend stall is discarded and has to be
re-fetched at 78% ready). Fetch alone could deliver 0.78 instr/cycle and the backend about 0.81,
yet measured IPC is 0.66. Two earlier attempts (r3s2 4-entry, r4s2 3-entry fetch queue) proved the
cycle side (-7.8% cycles, model matched silicon within 0.15%) but ranked as regressions because they
were built on a 59-68 MHz base and gave back 2-5% Fmax; LESSONS.md says to re-try only on top of the
fastest EX/MEM base. That base is now the champion (76.4 MHz, ~13 ns of cone budget).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small decoupled fetch queue between the predicted-PC fetch stream and ID, stacked on the
current champion (registered one-hot forwarding, split ctrl/data EX/MEM flops, registered kill). The
branch_predictor module (predecode of the fresh imem_data, JAL/BHT/RAS steering, RAS push/pop on
`fire`) is unchanged; EX, MEM, MDU, regfile and the BHT update path are untouched.

1. if_stage.sv: a 2-entry shift-register FIFO (head always entry 0), entries
   {pc[31:2], instr[31:0], pred_taken, pred_target[31:2], bht_cnt[1:0]} ~= 95 flops each. Only the
   occupancy register (2-bit thermometer, no adders) has a reset; queue data flops are
   enable-only (no reset, no bubble clear). `fire = imem_ready && !full && !kill` with `full` read
   from the occupancy flops only (occupancy before this cycle's pull, i.e. conservative, which is
   the behaviour the cycle model used). pc <= kill ? kill_target : fire ? next_pc : pc, so the PC
   enable no longer contains dmem_stall / load_use / mdu_stall and the late dmem_ready / MDU-done
   inputs leave the PC / imem-address register enable. branch_predictor `fire` input is wired to the
   same `fire`, so every instruction is predicted and RAS-pushed exactly once.
2. Decode source: head = empty ? {pc, imem_data, pred_*, valid = imem_ready && !kill} : queue[0]
   (valid = !kill). The empty-queue bypass keeps the fetch->EX latency and the 2-bubble registered-kill
   mispredict penalty of the champion; it is one 2:1 mux level in front of ID. Enqueue iff
   fire && !(empty && pull); dequeue iff pull && !empty. On `kill` the queue is flushed (occupancy
   <= 0) and nothing fires (kill outranks stall; kill_q stays held through a dmem stall as today).
3. hazard_unit.sv: load_use is computed on the HEAD instruction's rs1/rs2 against ID/EX (instead of
   raw io_imemData). `pull = head_valid && !dmem_stall && !mdu_stall && !load_use && !kill`;
   stall_id (ID/EX holds) = dmem_stall || mdu_stall; flush_id (bubble) = (load_use || kill ||
   !head_valid) && !dmem_stall; stall_if / flush_if are replaced by pull / head_valid. stall_ex_mem,
   hold_mem_wb and the MDU handshake are unchanged.
4. core.sv / id_stage.sv: wire pull / head_valid between hazard_unit and if_stage, feed if_id_t.valid
   from head_valid, and point the regfile read addresses, forward_unit select generation and the
   hazard compare at the head instruction instead of io_imemData. io_imemAddr stays the fetch PC.
5. Fmax protection rules (the whole point of retrying on this base): (a) no queue or occupancy
   signal may reach ex_stage / mem_stage / forwarding / ALU / dmem-address cones; the only coupling
   is `pull`, which feeds the existing ID/EX hold/bubble controls; (b) keep ID/EX sync-reset fan-out
   as in the champion (ctrl/valid only, data flops enable-only); (c) 2 entries rather than 3-4 to
   keep the flop count (~190) and the head-mux/pull fan-out small (the model gives 2 entries -6.3%
   cycles vs 4 entries -7.8%); (d) full/empty from registered occupancy only.

Expected: ~-6% cycles (4.43M -> ~4.15M) at Fmax within ~2% of 76.4 MHz, i.e. fitness ~180-185 vs the
172.4 champion. If the implementer finds the 2-entry version loses Fmax from the head-mux fan-out,
fall back to 1 entry plus bypass (model: -2.1% cycles) rather than growing the queue.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-003-r5s2 (regression, -0.77%): The r4s2-recommended retry of the decoupled fetch queue on the 76 MHz EX/MEM base (2 entries, empty-queue bypass, PC enable freed from dmem/MDU/load-use stalls, head-instruction regfile-read/forward-select/load-use compares, only `pull` touching ID/EX hold/bubble) landed at 171.1 vs the 172.4 champion, so the ~6% modeled cycle saving was apparently cancelled by Fmax/area cost even with the smallest queue and every Fmax-protection rule applied — with 4-, 3- and 2-entry versions now all failing on 59-76 MHz bases, treat front-end stall decoupling as exhausted (CoreMark's ~22% imem stalls plus a head mux ahead of ID are a wash at this clock) and only revisit if the Fmax/cycles split is measured and the head mux can be kept off the ID read/forward-select cone.

title: Fold JAL/JALR link into ID-premuxed op_b (ALU_LUI) and share one a_in+imm adder to trim the EX result tail
motivation:
The champion (90.64 MHz, 13 logic levels) has its worst path from
cpu/u_mem/reg_q.wb_data[4] (MEM/WB forward source) through the u_ex forward
mux and u_alu to cpu/u_ex/reg_q.alu_result[26]. After the 86->90 MHz regfile
fix every EX path launches from a fabric flop, so what is left is pure
EX-cone depth: forward mux -> ALU (adder/shifter/compare) -> ALU result case
mux -> `in.ctrl.is_jump ? pc+4 : ex_result` -> `| (is_mdu ? mdu_result : 0)`
-> alu_result D pin. The last two levels are not ALU work at all: the
JAL/JALR link value pc+4 does not depend on any forwarded operand, yet it is
muxed in *after* the ALU, and it needs its own 32-bit pc+4 carry chain in EX
next to the ALU adder, the AGU adder and a third identical a_in+imm adder
(jalr_sum == agu_sum) that all hang off the fan-out-15 a_in net. LESSONS say
the next Fmax lever is the ALU result-select / launch cone, and that
cycle-neutral changes which delete select levels or fan-out from a_in are
worth a few real percent (r3s1 +8.8%, r4s1 +12%, r5s0 +18.6%).

mux -> `in.ctrl.is_jump ? pc+4 : ex_result` -> `| (is_mdu ? mdu_result : 0)`
-> alu_result D pin. The last two levels are not ALU work at all: the
JAL/JALR link value pc+4 does not depend on any forwarded operand, yet it is
muxed in *after* the ALU, and it needs its own 32-bit pc+4 carry chain in EX
next to the ALU adder, the AGU adder and a third identical a_in+imm adder
(jalr_sum == agu_sum) that all hang off the fan-out-15 a_in net. LESSONS say
the next Fmax lever is the ALU result-select / launch cone, and that
cycle-neutral changes which delete select levels or fan-out from a_in are
worth a few real percent (r3s1 +8.8%, r4s1 +12%, r5s0 +18.6%).
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three cycle-neutral, bit-exact edits confined to id_stage / ex_stage / alu
(decoder, core_pkg encodings and the alu port list stay unchanged, so no
protected test helper is touched):

1. Link value computed in ID, not EX. In id_stage, for `dec_is_jump` force
   `ctrl_decoded.alu_op = ALU_LUI` and `reg_q.op_b <= in.pc + 32'd4`
   (a 30-bit incrementer fed only by the IF/ID pc flop, far shorter than the
   regfile-read -> op mux path that already ends at the same flop), and gate
   the b_ex/b_wb selects off for jumps (`sel2_ex && !dec_alu_src &&
   !dec_is_jump`; JAL's instr[24:20] bits are immediate bits and must not
   match a producer). EX then sees ALU_LUI (out = b_in = pc+4) for JAL/JALR

   (pc_plus4 for recover_target / pc_next stays). JALR's target already uses

title: Move the MEM/WB forward leg out of EX: capture the MEM-stage result into ID/EX operands
motivation:
The r5s0 champion (90.64 MHz) reports its worst path as
cpu/u_mem/reg_q.wb_data_4 -> cpu/u_ex/reg_q.alu_result_26 (16.6 ns, 13 LUT
levels). Every critical group (alu_result, kill_q, upd_taken_q) runs through the
EX operand forward mux a_in/b_in/s_in = ex_mem ? EX/MEM.alu_result : mem_wb ?
wb_data : ID/EX operand. Per bit that mux has 7 inputs (a_ex, ex_rw, a_wb,
mem_wb_reg_write, alu_result[i], wb_data[i], op_a[i]), i.e. 2 LUT levels in front
of the 32-bit carry chain, and the MEM/WB wb_data flop is the start point of the
worst path with a large fan-out (31 regfile write ports + 2 regfile bypass muxes +
three EX forward muxes per bit). Earlier wins were all of the form "take a late or
high-fan-out thing off the EX cone" (registered selects, registered kill, no
BSRAM launch); the 3-way forward mux itself was never reduced.
The MEM/WB -> EX leg is not needed in EX at all: the value it carries (the result
of the instruction currently in the MEM stage) already exists one cycle earlier,
combinationally, inside mem_stage (mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result), which is
exactly the value that is about to be written into MEM/WB.wb_data. The consumer
sits in ID at that moment and is about to be captured into ID/EX, so it can take
the value there (in the operand-capture mux that already exists for op_a/op_b/
rs2_val) rather than in EX one cycle later.
