hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cycle-neutral restructuring of forwarding (same coverage, same stalls, same
predictor, same retirement order):

1. mem_stage.sv: export the value it is about to latch into MEM/WB.wb_data as a new
   output `wb_next` (mem_to_reg ? load_data : in.alu_result), plus `wb_next_ok`
   = in.ctrl.reg_write && !mem_misalign (the post-trap reg_write that
   ctrl_with_trap already computes). core.sv wires them to id_stage.

2. forward_unit.sv: the ID-stage "wb" selects (sel1_wb/sel2_wb, the match of the
   ID instruction's rs1/rs2 against the instruction in EX/MEM, which is in the MEM
   stage this cycle) are additionally gated with wb_next_ok (trap-cancelled
   misaligned LOAD in MEM must not be forwarded; the older producer is then
   already covered by the regfile write-first bypass). The "ex" selects
   (match against the instruction in EX -> forwarded from EX/MEM next cycle) are
   unchanged, including the registered producer reg_write gate in EX for
   trap-cancelled JAL/JALR.

3. id_stage.sv: when sel*_wb is set, op_a / op_b / rs2_val are captured from
   `wb_next` instead of the regfile read (final 2:1 level driven by an early
   select; the auipc / alu_src gating of the a_/b_ selects is folded into the
   select so the late wb_next signal enters at the last LUT). Priority is
   MEM-stage producer > regfile write-first bypass (WB-stage producer) >
   regfile. Remove the registered a_wb/b_wb/s_wb flags from ID/EX (and from
   id_ex_t in core_pkg.sv); keep a_ex/b_ex/s_ex. ID/EX is not captured while
   stall_id (dmem stall, MDU) is high, and a bubble/kill capture is zero, so a
   capture only happens on a cycle where the MEM-stage instruction really
   completes and wb_next is valid; the load-use bubble still delays a consumer of
   a LOAD in EX by one cycle, after which the LOAD is in MEM and is captured via
   wb_next.

4. ex_stage.sv: a_in = a_use_ex ? fwd_ex_mem : in.op_a (same for b_in, s_in),
   where a_use_ex = in.a_ex && ex_rw. That is a 4-input function per bit, i.e. ONE
   LUT4 level instead of two, on every path into the ALU, the AGU adder, the
   branch comparators, jalr_hit and the MDU operand capture. The
   fwd_mem_wb/mem_wb_reg_write inputs are no longer used by the timed datapath
   (fwd_mem_wb remains only inside the RVFI-only rs1_rvfi legacy compare, which is
   pruned from the timed netlist and unchanged, so RVFI rs1_rdata stays exact).

Expected effect: one LUT level (~1.1-1.2 ns incl. routing) removed from the
16.6 ns forward->ALU->result / compare->kill_q cones (~7% Fmax), plus the wb_data
flop loses three of its loads. The new ID-side path (BSRAM DO -> byte align ->
mem_to_reg mux -> operand-capture mux -> ID/EX flop, ~2.3 + 5-6 LUTs) is
structurally shorter than the EX cone it replaces. Area: -3x(1 flop) for the
wb flags and one 32-bit mux leg per operand removed from EX but three 2:1 leg
added in ID, roughly neutral. The alu/decoder/imm_gen/reg_file/mdu module
interfaces (and hence the cocotb unit tests) are untouched; only
test_pipeline-visible behaviour must stay bit-identical, and the formal
(pc_fwd, reg, ill, liveness) and CoreMark cosim gates cover the trap-cancel
corner cases.

title: 1-cycle mispredict recovery (refetch target in the kill cycle) plus local-history two-level direction predictor
motivation:
Measured on the CoreMark trace (reference ISS, 2.94M retired instructions, 532K
conditional branches, 296K taken, 49.6K JAL, 13.8K ret, only 22 non-ret JALR): the
current 128x2b bimodal BHT (index pc[8:2]) mispredicts 54.9K branches (10.3%); JAL
and the 4-entry RAS are essentially perfect (12 ret misses). Every mispredict costs 2
cycles (registered kill: the wrong-path instruction fetched in the kill cycle is
thrown away), i.e. ~110K of the 4.43M cycles (2.5%). The remaining cycle budget is
fetch-bound (2.94M / 0.78 = 3.77M) plus load-use (205K), dmem stalls (~150K) and MUL
(94K x 2) stalls, none of which a predictor can touch, so the mispredict term is the
entire predictor-side lever (upper bound ~2.5%). A simulation of alternatives on the
real branch stream: bimodal 512 -> 40.2K misses; gshare is WORSE than bimodal here
(57.8K for 256x4b history, 50.5K for 1Kx8b) because CoreMark's hot branches are
loop/CRC branches with per-branch (local) patterns; a per-branch local-history
two-level predictor (256 x 8b history table, 4096 x 2b PHT indexed by
{hist,4'b0} ^ pc[13:2]) -> 24.6K misses (-55%); BHT update lag (carried counter,
update ~4 instructions after fetch) changes the miss count by <1%.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two cooperating changes, both confined to the fetch side so the EX/MEM Fmax cone
(16.6 ns, wb_data -> forward -> ALU -> alu_result) is untouched.

(A) Refetch the corrected target in the kill cycle. kill_q / kill_target_q are
already flops, and the timed bench drives imem_data from an LFSR flop, so a
flop->LUT->output mux on the fetch address costs ~1 LUT level. In if_stage define
fetch_pc = kill ? kill_target[31:2] : pc[31:2] and drive io_imemAddr, the predictor
`pc`, pc_plus4 and out.pc from it. In the kill cycle the instruction fetched at the
target is therefore a valid correct-path instruction: it is predicted/decoded like any
other and captured into ID/EX at the end of the kill cycle (while the wrong-path
instruction in EX is still turned into a bubble by kill_q, exactly as now). PC update:
if (kill) pc <= (imem_ready && !dmem_stall) ? next_pc : kill_target; else as before
(the fallback reproduces today's behaviour when the refetch cannot be consumed: imem
not ready, or a dmem stall holding kill/ID-EX). Required companion edits:
* flush_if = imem_stall only (kill no longer NOPs the F/D instruction); out.valid =
  !imem_stall.
* hazard_unit: mask load_use_hazard with !kill (the instruction in EX is wrong-path),
  so stall_if/stall_id/flush_id are not raised by it; flush_id = load_use && !dmem_stall
  only (kill no longer bubbles ID/EX; dmem_stall still holds ID/EX).
* branch_predictor `fire` = kill ? (imem_ready && !dmem_stall) : !stall, so RAS
  push/pop for the refetched instruction happens exactly once.
* Forwarding needs no change: the wrong-path EX instruction becomes a bubble with
  reg_write=0 at the next edge, ex_stage gates a_ex/b_ex/s_ex with the EX/MEM
  registered reg_write, and the *_wb selects (computed against the real older producers
  in EX/MEM / MEM/WB) are independent of *_ex. is_mdu is already gated with !kill.
Expected saving 0.78 cycle per mispredict (the refetch only helps when imem is ready
in the kill cycle).

(B) Replace the bimodal BHT in branch_predictor.sv with a local two-level predictor:
LHT = 256 x 8b per-branch history (no reset LUT-RAM, index fetch_pc[9:2]); PHT = 4096 x
2b counters (no reset LUT-RAM), index = {lhist[7:0], 4'b0000} ^ fetch_pc[13:2]. Both
are async-read LUT-RAM; the path is pc/kill mux -> LHT read -> XOR -> PHT read -> MSB
-> pred_taken -> next_pc, ~7-8 LUT levels, well under the 11 ns cycle and not shared
with the EX cone. The carried bundle replaces bht_cnt[1:0] with {lhist[7:0], cnt[1:0]}
in if_id_t / id_ex_t; on a retiring branch EX sends upd_valid, upd_taken, upd_cnt,
upd_hist and pc[13:2] (from in.pc) through the existing registered update stage;
the update writes LHT[pc[9:2]] <= {hist[6:0], taken} and PHT[({hist,4'b0}^pc[13:2])] <=
saturating inc/dec of the carried counter. Static JAL/ret prediction, RAS and the
misaligned/out-of-range rules are unchanged. If the 4096-entry PHT hurts Fmax, drop to
2048 entries (index {hist[7:0],3'b0}^pc[12:2], 28K misses) or just ship (A).

Net modelled effect: mispredict cost 110K cycles -> ~24.6K x 1.22 = 30K cycles, i.e.
~80K of 4.43M cycles (-1.8%) at unchanged Fmax. This is honestly below the 4.6%
acceptance bar on its own; it is the largest predictor-side improvement the measured
branch stream allows, and (A) is nearly free in area.

title: Cut the ID-capture cone: one-hot pre-decoded load lanes, wb_next at the last LUT, reset-free ID/EX data flops
motivation:
`make timing` on the r6s1 champion (placement 0, 90.6 MHz; 99.9 MHz median) shows
the top-25 setup paths all within ~0.3 ns of each other (data delay 10.7-11.0 ns)
and the majority END IN THE ID STAGE OPERAND-CAPTURE FLOPS (op_a/op_b/rs2_val):
  1. dmem BSRAM DO[7] -> wb_next -> id_stage -> op_b_20      (11.00 ns)
     = BSRAM clk->DO 2.26 ns, then 8 serial LUT4s: wb_next_Z_31_s4 -> s3 -> s2 -> s0
     (a 4-deep chain just to build the load SIGN bit, fan-out 16), wb_next_Z_20_s,
     rs2_nxt_20_s24 -> rs2_nxt_20_s0 -> op_b_nxt_20_s0. Route is 5.5 of the 11.0 ns.
  2. lfsr (instr rs2 bits) -> regfile read -> op_b_2 / op_b_16 / rs2_val_16 (10.98 ns):
     select decode (fan-out 32, one net with 2.8 ns of routing) then a 5-LUT tail
     s13 -> s6 -> s2 -> s1 -> s22 into rs2_val.
  3. kill_q -> ... -> op_a_5/21/22/23/25 (10.74-10.95 ns): kill_q drives flush_if
     (NOP-mux on the F/D instruction -> decoder -> a_use_rf) and flush_id, the
     synchronous clear of all ~300 ID/EX data flops.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cycle-neutral re-expression of three pieces of logic (no cycle, stall or RVFI change).

1. Pre-decoded one-hot load lanes (ex_stage + core_pkg + mem_stage).
   In EX, compute from the registered ID/EX ctrl (mem_width, mem_sext, mem_read) and
   agu_sum[1:0] (low carry-chain bits, early; the adder is not lengthened) a small set
   of one-hot selects and register them in EX/MEM next to mem_addr (data flops, hold on
   dmem stall, no reset): ld_l0..ld_l3 (result[7:0] <- rdata byte lane; word and
   half@0 -> l0, half@2 -> l2), ld_hlo / ld_hhi (result[15:8] <- rdata[15:8] for
   word/half@0, rdata[31:24] for half@2), ld_w (result[31:16] <- rdata[31:16], word
   only), sg0..sg3 (sign source r[7]/r[15]/r[23]/r[31], pre-gated with mem_sext and
   the width: byte@0 / byte@1,half@0 / byte@2 / byte@3,half@2) and ld_ext (fill
   [31:8] byte / [31:16] half with the sign). All are ANDed with mem_read, so they are
   0 for non-loads. In mem_stage replace shifted/byte_val/hword_val/width-case/sext
   and the mem_to_reg mux with a plain AND-OR: sign halves s_a = sg0&r7 | sg1&r15 and
   s_b = sg2&r23 | sg3&r31 (one LUT4 each, straight from the BSRAM pins), and for
   bits [31:16]: wb_next[i] = ld_w&r[i] | !mem_to_reg&alu_result[i] | ld_ext&(s_a|s_b)
   (a LUT4 whose late inputs are s_a, s_b). Bits [15:8] and [7:0] are the same shape
   with the lane selects. The rdata -> wb_next depth drops from ~5 serial LUTs to 2.
   wb_next_ok, the misalign gating of dmem_wen/ren, aligned_addr and every RVFI
   mem_* field stay bit-identical (MEM/WB.mem_rdata is RVFI-only, pruned from the
   timed netlist).

2. Capture muxes with wb_next at the last LUT (id_stage). Pre-combine every early
   source and give the late values their own last stage:
     use_wbn_a = sel1_wb && !dec_is_auipc;  use_wbn_b = sel2_wb && !dec_alu_src;
     use_wbn_s = sel2_wb;
     early_a = dec_is_auipc ? in.pc : wb_data;  early_b = dec_alu_src ? imm : wb_data;
     sel_early_a = dec_is_auipc || rs1_byp;  sel_early_b = dec_alu_src || rs2_byp;
     sel_early_s = rs2_byp;
     op_x_nxt = use_wbn_x ? wb_next : (sel_early_x ? early_x : rs*_raw)
   i.e. wb_next goes through exactly one LUT before the flop (previously three) and
   the regfile read enters a 3-input LUT, one level shallower than the
   s13..s22 tail seen in the regfile path. Same priority as today (MEM-stage
   producer > write-first bypass > regfile; pc/imm override both bypasses). If the
   placer prefers the rs*_raw late instead, the alternative association
   `(use_wbn_x|sel_early_x) ? (use_wbn_x ? wb_next : early_x) : rs*_raw` can be
   tried; `make timing` takes ~35 s so both can be measured. Also drive use_wbn_*
   / sel_early_* from the un-flushed io_imemData address compare only (as now) so
   the NOP-gate stays off them.

3. Reset/flush-free ID/EX data flops (id_stage). `if (reset || flush) reg_q <= '0`
   currently puts kill_q -> flush_id on the clear of every ID/EX flop. Only ctrl,
   valid and the registered bypass selects a_ex/b_ex/s_ex need clearing (bubble
   must have reg_write=0, mem_*=0, is_branch/is_jump=0, valid=0, no forward select);

   consumer of those fields is gated by the registered ctrl/valid; kill_q update,
   bht_upd_valid, mispredict and is_mdu all already include in.valid or ctrl bits).

   tried this together with a shared-comparator change that cost Fmax; here the
   branch comparator and `case` are left alone.)

title: Pre-decode load lane/sign selects and misalign in EX; flat AND-OR MEM-result capture in ID
motivation:
The r6s1 champion (99.9 MHz, 225.3) reports its worst path as the dmem BSRAM
DO -> cpu/u_mem -> cpu/u_id/reg_q.op_b_* (16.3 ns, 9 cells, ~8 LUT levels after
the 2.3 ns BSRAM clk->DO launch). That is the path r6s1 itself created by
moving the MEM-stage result into the ID operand capture. In RTL that cone is:
DO -> shifted = rdata >> (addr[1:0]*8) (a 4:1 byte mux, 2 levels) -> byte/half
sign select by width+sext (1-2 levels, then fan-out 24 to every upper bit) ->
width case -> wb_next = mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result -> s_early =
sel2_wb ? wb_next : wb_data -> b_early = alu_src ? imm : s_early -> op_b_nxt =
b_use_rf ? rs2_raw : b_early. The late BSRAM data therefore passes through
~3 mux levels in id_stage plus ~4 in mem_stage even though every select
(addr[1:0], mem_width, mem_sext, mem_to_reg, sel*_wb, alu_src) is known a whole
stage earlier than the data. The sel*_wb selects are additionally gated with
wb_next_ok, which is computed combinationally in MEM from mem_misalign
(mem_addr[1:0] + width compare) on top of the registered ctrl.
Prior wins in this slot (r3s1, r4s1, r6s1: +9%, +12%, +10%) were all "resolve
selects one stage early, let the late value enter at the last LUT". The load
data path has not had that treatment yet; it is now the single limiter that
every other recent path group (u_rf -> u_id, EX forward -> ALU -> result) is
within ~1-2 ns of, so shortening it by several levels moves Fmax until the next
group takes over.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cycle-neutral restructuring (same stalls, same forwarding coverage, same
predictor, identical retirement/RVFI values):

1. ex_stage.sv + core_pkg.sv (ex_mem_t): compute the load-extraction selects in
   EX from the AGU adder's low bits (agu_sum[1:0], the first bits out of the
   carry chain, so they are early) and the decoded ctrl.mem_width/mem_sext, and
   register them in EX/MEM as plain data-block flops (no reset/bubble, same
   !stall enable as the other EX/MEM data fields): one-hot byte-source selects
   for result bits [7:0] (ld_s0[3:0]: which of the four BSRAM bytes), for bits
   [15:8] (word/half-lo -> byte1, half-hi -> byte3, byte -> extension), a
   "word passes through bits [31:16]" select, and one-hot sign-source selects
   ld_sg[3:0] (= sext & the byte whose bit 7 is the sign for the byte/half
   case; all zero for zero-extend and for word loads). Also register
   mem_misalign_q (misalign computed in EX from agu_sum[1:0] and mem_width) and
   wb_ok_q = ctrl_with_trap.reg_write && !misalign, so mem_stage's trap gating
   and wb_next_ok become flop outputs (no compare in MEM; the ctrl/valid
   reset/bubble block is unchanged). RVFI-visible values (mem_rmask/wmask,
   aligned mem_addr, trap) are still produced exactly as today from the
   registered misalign.

2. mem_stage.sv: replace `shifted = rdata >> (addr[1:0]*8)` + width case +
   sign/zero-extend with a flat AND-OR driven by the registered one-hot
   selects: load_data[7:0] = OR_k(ld_s0[k] & rdata[8k+7:8k]); load_data[15:8] =
   (ld_h1 & rdata[15:8]) | (ld_h3 & rdata[31:24]) | {8{sign}}; load_data[31:16]
   = (ld_w ? rdata[31:16] : {16{sign}}), where sign = OR_k(ld_sg[k] &
   rdata[8k+7]) (a 4-way AND-OR: two LUT4 levels, ONE copy per upper-bit
   group so the fan-out is 24 not on a long mux tree). BSRAM data thus sees
   2-3 LUT levels instead of ~5. Also export the pieces separately
   (`ld_data`, `alu_res`, `m2r_q`) so id_stage can do the final select.

3. id_stage.sv: rewrite op_a/op_b/rs2_val capture as a flat one-hot AND-OR
   with all selects computed from early signals only (registered ex_mem
   ctrl/mem_to_reg/wb_ok_q, the sel*_wb compares, alu_src, is_auipc, rs*_byp):
     op_b_nxt = (rs2_raw & use_rf) | (ld_data & use_ld) | (alu_res & use_alu)
              | (imm & use_imm) | (wb_data & use_wbd)
   with use_ld = sel2_wb & m2r_q & !alu_src, use_alu = sel2_wb & !m2r_q &
   !alu_src etc. (one-hot by construction, priority MEM producer > regfile
   write-first bypass > regfile preserved). The BSRAM-derived ld_data and the
   regfile-mux rs*_raw both enter at the last LUT level (final OR of a
   pre-merged early term plus one AND term), so the post-BSRAM depth in
   id_stage drops from ~3 levels to 1. Same for op_a (is_auipc -> pc term) and
   rs2_val (s_*). MEM/WB.wb_data flop D = m2r_q ? ld_data : alu_res as today
   (one extra LUT level there is off the critical cone since it ends at a
   flop D without further logic).

4. forward_unit.sv: wb_next_ok input is now the registered wb_ok_q (port name
   unchanged); everything else unchanged. hazard_unit/alu/decoder/imm_gen/
   reg_file/mdu/branch_predictor and the core's top-level IO are untouched, so
   the cocotb unit tests (test_alu/decoder/imm_gen/reg_file/mdu) are unaffected
   and test_pipeline.py only lists source files.

Expected effect: ~3-4 LUT levels (~4-5 ns incl. routing/fan-out) removed from
the BSRAM -> u_mem -> u_id cone, which drops from 16.3 ns to roughly 12-13 ns,
so that group stops being the worst. Fmax then becomes limited by the next
group (u_rf -> u_id regfile read and EX forward -> ALU -> result/kill_q,
both a bit under 16 ns after r6s1), estimated +8% Fmax at identical cycle
count. Area: ~12 extra EX/MEM flops, AND-OR replacing muxes; roughly LUT
neutral. Risk: the new selects add one LUT after agu_sum[1:0] in EX (low bits
of the adder, short) and the id_stage select fan-out grows (one-hot selects
with fan-out 32 each); if the implementer sees the select nets becoming
critical they should duplicate the select flops per 16-bit half.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-002-r7s1 (regression, -1.29%): Pre-decoding the load lane/sign selects and misalign/`wb_ok` in EX into one-hot EX/MEM flops, with a flat AND-OR load align and a one-hot `op_a`/`op_b`/`rs2_val` capture in ID, was cycle-neutral but left Fmax flat (222.4 vs the 225.3 champion, not the +8% estimated) and sibling r7s0 (same one-hot load-lane idea) fell -6.3% with its worst path just moving to regfile read -> `u_id` `op_a` capture (16.2 ns), so every r6/r7 critical group (BSRAM -> `u_mem` -> `u_id`, `u_rf` -> `u_id`, `wb_data` -> ALU -> `alu_result`) sits at ~16.2-16.5 ns and shortening the load-align cone alone cannot move Fmax — a gain needs two or more of these cones cut together, and since r6s1's 99.9 MHz was one lucky seed (others 90.6) a ~1% delta is inside place-and-route noise.

title: Retry 1-cycle mispredict recovery plus local-history direction predictor on the r6s1 99.9 MHz base
motivation:
Measured on the CoreMark trace (r6s2 analysis, reference ISS: 2.94M retired
instructions, 532K conditional branches, 296K taken, 49.6K JAL, 13.8K ret, only
22 non-ret JALR): the current 128x2b bimodal BHT (index pc[8:2]) mispredicts
54.9K branches (10.3%); JAL and the 4-entry RAS are essentially perfect. Every
mispredict costs 2 cycles (registered kill: the instruction fetched in the kill
cycle is a dropped wrong-path/NOP slot), i.e. ~110K of the 4.43M cycles (2.5%).
The rest of the cycle budget (fetch-bound 2.94M/0.78, load-use 205K, dmem 150K,
MUL 188K) is not predictor-addressable, so mispredict cost is the whole
predictor lever. The previous attempt at exactly this (r6s2: refetch in the kill
cycle + 256x8b local history / 4096x2b PHT) scored 214.87 vs 204.51 (+5.07%) on
the r5s0 base, but lost the round to r6s1 (+10.18%, MEM-leg moved into ID), and
LESSONS explicitly recommends re-trying it on the r6s1 base. It is orthogonal to
the r6s1 change (EX forward cone, id_stage operand capture), which it does not
touch. Accuracy simulation on the real branch stream: gshare is WORSE than
bimodal here (57.8K misses) because the hot CoreMark branches are loop/CRC
branches with per-branch patterns; bimodal-512 -> 40.2K; per-branch local
history (256x8b LHT, 4096x2b PHT) -> 24.6K, 2048-entry PHT -> ~28K.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two cooperating fetch-side changes. The EX/MEM Fmax cone (forward -> ALU ->
alu_result / compare -> kill_q) and the r6s1 ID operand-capture path are
untouched; the only effect on them is that `kill` leaves the F/D NOP mux and the
ID/EX flush, which are fan-out-heavy nets feeding the ~300 ID/EX flops.

(A) Refetch the corrected target in the kill cycle (1-cycle penalty instead of 2).
kill_q/kill_target_q are flops already. In if_stage define
fetch_pc = kill ? kill_target[31:2] : pc[31:2] and drive io_imemAddr, the
predictor's pc input, pc_plus4 and out.pc from it. The instruction fetched at
the target in the kill cycle is then a valid correct-path instruction: it is
predicted/decoded normally and captured into ID/EX at the end of the kill cycle,
while the wrong-path instruction in EX is still bubbled by kill_q exactly as now.
PC update: if (kill) pc <= stall ? kill_target : next_pc; else if (!stall)
pc <= next_pc (when the refetch cannot be consumed - imem not ready or a dmem
stall holding kill / ID/EX - this reproduces today's behaviour and the target is
simply refetched next cycle). Companion edits:
  * hazard_unit: flush_if = imem_stall only (kill no longer NOPs F/D; if_stage
    out.valid = !flush); mask load_use_hazard with !kill (the instruction in EX

title: LUT-RAM register file with written-bit zero gating: drop ~1000 flops and the 32:1 flop read mux
motivation:
CoreMark is already at the ~22%-imem-stall fetch bound (2.94M retired instructions
/ 0.78 = 3.77M of the 4.43M cycles), so every remaining gain is Fmax. r7s0/r7s1
showed the critical groups are tied at ~16.2-16.5 ns arrival: dmem BSRAM -> u_mem
-> u_id operand capture, regfile read (lfsr instr bits -> 32:1 mux) -> u_id
operand capture, and the EX/MEM.alu_result forward -> ALU -> alu_result cone. Half
of every path is routing (r7s0: 5.5 of 11.0 ns), and trimming one cone just moves
the worst path to the next one, so a change has to shorten the regfile cone AND
shrink the netlist that all three cones are routed through.
reg_file.sv (r5s0) is 31 x 32 fabric flops with sync reset and CE (992 of the 1839
FFs) plus two 32:1 flop read muxes (~600-700 LUT4 each, 4-5 LUT/MUX levels deep
into the op_a/op_b/rs2_val capture mux). A 32x32 two-read-port file is exactly the
shape Gowin's distributed RAM (RAM16SDP4 / SSRAM, async read, sync write) holds in
~32 CLS: address -> DO is one LUT-ish delay, and the 5th address bit is one more
mux level. r5s0's BSRAM problem does not apply: SSRAM output is combinational, so
nothing launches at 2.3 ns clk->DO and no ID/EX flop is absorbed (the read data
goes through the capture mux, not straight into a flop; the BHT array already
infers LUT-RAM fine - lutram=8 in every result).

title: LUT-RAM (SSRAM) register file plus flat one-hot load capture: cut the regfile and BSRAM ID-capture cones together
motivation:
CoreMark/MHz is already near the fetch bound (one 32-bit imem word per cycle, ~22%
imem stalls; cycles are 4.43M in every recent run) and predictor / fetch-queue /
mispredict-recovery work is exhausted, so fitness is now purely Fmax. The log shows two
ID-capture cones tied at the top: BSRAM dmem DO -> u_mem load align -> u_id op_a/op_b/
rs2_val capture (r6s1: 16.3 ns arrival, 9 cells; r7s1 flattened it to 6 cells / 15.1 ns
and got 98.6-101.6 MHz) and regfile read -> u_id op_a capture (r7s0 moved the worst path
there, 16.2 ns, and lost 6%). Each prior attempt cut one cone and was capped by the other
(LESSONS r7s1: "a gain needs two or more of these cones cut together"). The regfile is
also the biggest structure in the timed netlist: 31x32 = 992 of 1839 flops (each with
sync reset + CE), ~650 LUTs of 32:1 read mux, each rs address bit fans out to ~256 mux
inputs and each wb_data bit to 31 flop D pins. r5s0 showed BSRAM inference is wrong for
the regfile (clk->DO launch tax, absorbs ID/EX flops), but Gowin distributed RAM (SSRAM,
RAM16SDP4: async read, synchronous write, no output register) is a different resource:
one LUT-class read delay, nothing to absorb. The run reports `lutram: 8` today (the 128x2
BHT), so SSRAM is already inferred correctly in this flow.

992 fabric flops. Ports, async-read timing, write-at-clock-edge and the write-first
rs*_byp match flags are unchanged (id_stage / core.sv need no changes), so CPI is
identical. One storage copy per read port (SSRAM has one read port per copy; both copies
take the same w_en/w_addr/w_data). Each copy is two 16-entry banks

wb_data to 4 write-data pins per bit instead of 31 flop D pins, the read path loses ~2 LUT
levels, and the design drops ~1000 flops / ~600 LUTs, which tightens placement for every
other cone. Write enables go to bank/copy write-enable pins (w_nz && w_addr[4] == bank).

INIT=0 in the bitstream, constant init for Verilator/Yosys), which also keeps slot 0 (never
written; w_nz drops x0 writes) reading 0 and power-up registers equal to the ISS's zeros,

An ISS profile of the 2K CoreMark trace (2.94M insns, 4.43M cycles, CPI 1.51) shows the
usual predictor levers are capped. Conditional-branch mispredicts are ~55K (10% of 532K
branches, ~110K cycles = 2.5%); a bigger/local-history PHT bought ~0 (r6s2/r7s2); and
there are only 22 non-ret JALRs in the whole run (13.8K rets, all handled by the RAS), so
an indirect-target cache is worthless. The one front-end lever with a measured cycle win
is decoupling the predicted fetch stream from backend stalls: the 2-entry queue of r5s2
cut cycles 4.43M -> 4.15M (-6.3%) but lost it all in Fmax (71 vs 75 MHz) because its head
mux sat in front of the ID regfile-read / forward-select / load-use cone. Those queues
were combinational at the ID side. The fix is to make the queue head a real F/D pipeline
register, so the mux moves to the flop D pin and every ID-side cone starts at a flop.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make IF/ID a registered stage (fd_pc, fd_instr, fd_valid, fd_pred_taken, fd_pred_target,
fd_bht_cnt) plus one skid slot of the same fields, both in if_stage.sv. The predictor stays
at fetch time exactly as today (predecode of imem_data, JAL/BHT/RAS, zero-bubble taken
prediction into the PC flop), so there is no taken-branch bubble. Flow control:
  pull     = ID consumes the F/D entry this cycle (!stall_id && !load_use) - from flops only.
  fetch    = imem_ready && !kill; the fetched word goes to F/D if F/D is empty or pulled this
             cycle and the skid is empty, otherwise into the skid. If the skid is occupied
             the PC holds (fire = fetch accepted, which also gates RAS push/pop as today).
  F/D next = skid_valid ? skid : (fetch ? imem word : empty); skid drains into F/D on pull.
rs1/rs2 regfile addresses, decoder, imm_gen, forward_unit compares and the load-use compare
all read the F/D flop outputs (fd_instr), so the imem_ready/NOP-gating (flush_if) and
imem_data -> regfile-read cones that lfsr-launched paths showed at 16.2-16.3 ns in
r6s0/r7s0 are replaced by flop-launched ones; the select mux (skid vs imem_data) ends at
the F/D flop D pin. kill (registered EX mispredict) clears F/D and the skid and loads the PC
from kill_target as today; since the wrong path now has one more instruction in flight the
mispredict penalty rises from 2 to 3 cycles (~+55K cycles, +1.2%), which the queue absorbs:
F/D+skid hold two fetched instructions across a dmem/MDU/load-use stall, so the ~22% imem
stall bubbles that currently re-roll every time the pipeline resumes are hidden while the
buffer is non-empty (r5s2 measured -6.3% cycles for the same capacity). Net modeled cycle
saving ~5%, with Fmax expected neutral-to-better because only flop outputs feed ID. Keep
reset/bubble clearing on fd_valid only (data flops ungated), the BHT update path and EX
prediction check unchanged, and do not touch ex_stage/mem_stage/forward cones.

title: Cut load-align and regfile-read cones together: LUT-RAM regfile with written-bit gate plus one-hot load lanes
motivation:
Every critical group on the r6s1 base sits at ~15-16.5 ns and is tied: dmem BSRAM DO -> u_mem load
align -> wb_next -> u_id operand capture; regfile read -> u_id op_a/op_b capture; and EX/MEM-forward
-> ALU -> alu_result. Prior attempts cut ONE cone at a time and the worst path just moved to the
next one (r7s1 one-hot load lanes: 222.4 flat; r7s0 -6.3%; r8s0 LUT-RAM regfile + written gate:
231.05, +2.5%, the best Fmax so far at 102.4 MHz but inside the P&R seed spread). LESSONS r7s1 says
a gain needs two or more cones cut together. r8s1 tried exactly that combination but died in formal
because of a constant `initial` zero-fill loop on the memory arrays, not because of the idea.

-> ALU -> alu_result. Prior attempts cut ONE cone at a time and the worst path just moved to the
next one (r7s1 one-hot load lanes: 222.4 flat; r7s0 -6.3%; r8s0 LUT-RAM regfile + written gate:
231.05, +2.5%, the best Fmax so far at 102.4 MHz but inside the P&R seed spread). LESSONS r7s1 says

because of a constant `initial` zero-fill loop on the memory arrays, not because of the idea.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Combine the two independently-validated cone cuts WITHOUT the `initial` zero-fill that broke r8s1.
(1) reg_file.sv: replace the 31x32 flop regfile and the two 32:1 read muxes with two
syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram" 32x32 arrays (one per read port, both written with the same
w_en/w_addr/w_data; no reset, no initial block) plus a 31-bit `written` flop vector (reset to 0,
set when a nonzero register is written). A read of a register whose `written` bit is 0 returns 0
(and x0 always 0), so the reset-to-zero architectural behaviour is preserved bit-exactly with only
flops for power-up state, which is what kept r8s0 formal-clean. rs1_raw/rs2_raw keep the same
interface so id_stage and core.sv do not change. The write-first bypass flags stay as they are.
(2) mem_stage.sv / ex_stage.sv: pre-decode the load lane selects in EX into a few one-hot EX/MEM
flops (byte lane 0..3 for byte loads, half select low/high, word, sign-enable) so the load align is a
flat AND-OR of dmem_rdata bytes under flop-driven one-hot selects (sign bit picked by the same
one-hot), with mem_to_reg folded in as another one-hot term, instead of shift-by-addr*8 followed by
width/sext case muxes. Keep the post-trap reg_write (wb_next_ok) computation exact: compute
misalign in EX from agu_sum[1:0] and mem_width and register it (ctrl_with_trap path in ex_stage,
after the existing ctrl_with_trap) so the MEM stage only reads flops; dmem_wen/dmem_ren gating must
still use the misalign-cleared enables so the trap-cancelled access never reaches the bus.
(3) id_stage.sv: fold the load align directly into the ID/EX operand capture. Evidence from log.jsonl:
the worst path of r6s1, r7s1, r8s0 and r8s2 is always dmem BSRAM DO -> cpu/u_mem -> cpu/u_id
reg_q.op_b / rs2_val (arrival 15.1-16.5 ns, 6-9 cells), whatever the regfile looks like, so the
BSRAM output must see as few LUT levels as possible. Instead of wb_next = align(rdata) feeding the
s_early/b_early/op_*_nxt muxes, build each captured bit as a flat AND-OR whose load terms are
(lane_k & sel_wb & rdata[8k+i]) for k=0..3 plus the early term (non-load / regfile / pc / imm / wb_data
selected by flop- or instruction-bit-driven selects that already exist). All lane/sign/width/misalign
selects come from the registered one-hot EX/MEM flops combined with the early sel*_wb compare, so
dmem_rdata passes through at most two LUT levels (AND-OR of 4 lanes, then merge with the early term
via MUX2_LUT5) before the op_a/op_b/rs2_val D pin. The sign-extend bits (31:8) use the registered
sign-enable one-hot AND the selected lane's MSB. Keep the wb_data flop path (MEM/WB) as it is.
Ordering/forwarding semantics are unchanged (cycle count identical, 4,431,994).
Success criterion: top-path report no longer lists u_mem -> u_id or u_rf -> u_id as the worst
group, so Fmax becomes limited only by the ALU cone; target >= 106 MHz median (> +4.6% vs 225.33).
If the implementer has time, also leave alu.sv/core_pkg encodings untouched (test_alu.py and
test/_helpers.py mirror them) and do not touch the reset/CE structure of other pipeline registers.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-001-r9s0 (regression, -6.16%): Stacking the two individually-validated cone cuts (r8s0 distributed-RAM regfile + `written` zero-gate, r7s1 EX-registered one-hot load lanes, plus folding the lane AND-OR directly into the ID/EX `op_a`/`op_b`/`rs2_val` capture) was cycle-neutral and formal-clean but scored 211.44, below both parts (231.05, 222.4) and the 225.33 champion, which refutes the r7s1 "cut two or more cones together" prescription — cutting cones does not add up here, and replicating ~13 one-hot select flops across three 32-bit capture muxes probably adds fan-out/routing that cancels the removed LUT levels, so with BSRAM clk->DO plus routing a likely ~15 ns floor and ~10% seed spread, stop restructuring the regfile/load-align cones and only try Fmax ideas backed by a `make timing` top-path report.

title: Resolve branch/JALR in MEM from registered operands: take compare, target and trap checks off the EX forward network
motivation:
After r6s1 the EX forward mux is one LUT4 per bit, but a_in / s_in still fan out
to the ALU, the AGU adder, three 32-bit branch comparators (EQ, signed LT,
unsigned LT, each with a 6-way case select), the JALR sum, the jalr_hit
(a_in == pred_target) compare, the MDU capture and the EX/MEM operand flops.
The branch-resolve cone (a_in/s_in -> compare -> mispredict -> kill_q /
upd_taken_q D pins) and the forward -> ALU -> alu_result cone were repeatedly
measured tied at the top of `make timing` (r5s1: both 18.57 ns), and every
earlier Fmax win was "take a late or high-fan-out consumer off the operand
nets". Single-cone trims were inside the ~10% place-and-route seed spread
(r7s1, r8s0), so this proposal removes a whole class of consumers at once.
EX/MEM already registers everything MEM-stage resolution needs: rs1_val and
rs2_val (post-forward operands, reg_q.rs1_val/rs2_val), mem_addr (the AGU sum
a_in + imm, which is exactly the JALR target before bit-0 clearing),
branch_target (pc + imm) and pc. So the branch can be resolved one stage later
from flops with no new datapath state.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move branch/jump resolution from EX to MEM (structural, no new predictor).

1. ex_stage.sv: delete the three branch comparators, `branch_cond`,
   `branch_taken`, `jalr_hit`, `jalr_sum`, the misalign_branch/jump checks and
   the mispredict/kill logic from EX. a_in/s_in now feed only the ALU, the AGU
   adder, the MDU and the EX/MEM operand flops (fan-out from ~15 to ~6 per
   bit). EX/MEM additionally registers `pred_taken`, `pred_target`, `bht_cnt`
   and the branch_op/is_branch/is_jalr/is_jump ctrl bits (already in ctrl).
   branch_target (pc + imm) and pc+4 stay computed in EX (adders on registered
   ID/EX fields, off the forward network). ex_result/alu_result for JAL/JALR
   (pc+4) is unchanged.

2. mem_stage.sv (or a new rtl/branch_resolve.sv instantiated from core.sv):
   in MEM compute branch_cond from the EX/MEM registered rs1_val/rs2_val using
   the same six-way case select (flop -> compare -> mispredict, ~5 cells), the
   JALR target from mem_addr (a_in + imm, registered; bit 0 cleared, bits[1:0]
   != 0 -> misaligned), the misalign trap (misalign_branch: taken && target[1:0]
   != 0; misalign_jump) merged into the existing `ctrl_with_trap` (is_illegal=1,
   reg_write=0) that mem_stage already builds for the misaligned-load/store trap,
   and RVFI pc_next (misalign ? pc+4 : jump ? target : taken ? branch_target :
   pc+4). The prediction check keeps its exact rules from ex_stage (branch:
   direction differs; JAL: !pred_taken && !misalign_jump; JALR: RAS-hit compare
   of mem_addr against {pred_target,2'b00} or an unpredicted aligned-by-bit-1
   JALR), the recovery target is chosen from registered fields, and
   {kill_q, kill_target_q} are latched from MEM instead of EX. Recovery penalty
   goes from 2 to 3 cycles (about +1.2% cycles: ~55K mispredicts in 4.43M).

3. Wrong-path squash. When a branch in MEM mispredicts, the instruction behind
   it is in EX and the one behind that in ID (and F/D) -- all wrong path.
   The registered kill_q now has to bubble the instruction that moves EX -> MEM
   in the kill cycle AND clear the instruction that has just moved into MEM:
   because kill_q is a flop, gate the MEM instruction's side effects with it in
   the *next* cycle: dmem_wen/dmem_ren/ctrl.reg_write/valid for the MEM
   instruction are ANDed with !kill_q (flop outputs, one extra LUT input on the
   dmem write-enable pins and on MEM/WB valid/reg_write; wb_next_ok also gets
   !kill_q so a squashed producer is not forwarded). The EX instruction in the
   kill cycle is bubbled exactly as today (EX/MEM ctrl/valid <= 0 on kill_q),
   the F/D instruction is NOP'd by flush_if, ID/EX is flushed by flush_id.
   Hold kill_q across a dmem stall as today. ID/EX bubble on kill and the
   `!kill` gate on MDU `active` stay (a wrong-path M-op in EX at the kill cycle
   must not start the MDU). A wrong-path M-op must also never be *in flight*
   when the kill arrives (a 35-cycle divide would otherwise keep the MDU busy
   and a correct-path op would sample stale operands), so the M-op is held in
   EX (is_mdu && !done, counted in mdu_stall, `active` gated) for the one cycle
   that an unresolved branch/jump sits in MEM (is_branch|is_jump in EX/MEM ctrl,
   a registered bit). This costs a cycle only for an M-op directly behind a
   branch/jump and keeps mdu.sv and its ports (test_mdu.py) unchanged.

4. Forward gating for misaligned JAL/JALR: the producer's trap now happens in
   MEM, so ex_rw (EX forward gate from the registered EX/MEM reg_write) must
   also drop when the MEM instruction is a misaligned jump
   (is_jump && mem_addr[1:0] != 0, a 2-bit check on EX/MEM flops folded into
   the a_use_ex/b_use_ex/s_use_ex LUT) and wb_next_ok already includes the
   MEM-stage reg_write after the trap.

5. BHT update: bht_upd_valid/idx/taken/cnt come from MEM (upd_taken_q register
   stage in branch_predictor already absorbs the late compare; nothing else
   in the predictor changes).

Cycle-wise the only change is the +1 recovery cycle; the dmem path, load-use,
MDU and predictor are untouched. Fmax-wise EX loses the compare/mispredict/kill
endpoints and ~9 loads per a_in/s_in bit, and the new MEM cone is registered
operands -> carry-chain compare -> mispredict -> kill_q D, structurally shorter
than the EX cone it replaces (no forward mux, no AGU/ALU sharing the nets).
Expected: ~+7% Fmax at -1.2% cycles, net ~+5%.
Verification: riscv-formal checks (pc_fwd, insn, ill, liveness) cover the trap
and next-pc semantics; cocotb test_alu.py is untouched (alu.sv unchanged).
Keep core_pkg.sv ALU/ctrl encodings and the alu/decoder/imm_gen/reg_file/mdu
ports unchanged (r3s0 lesson: protected test helpers mirror them). Extra
id_ex_t / ex_mem_t fields are internal to rtl/ and safe.

title: Fetch-time indirect-jump target cache: predict non-ret JALR (jump-table jr, function-pointer calls) from a 16-entry last-target LUT-RAM updated from EX/MEM
motivation:
Prior predictor rounds are exhausted on direction accuracy and recovery latency: r6s2 (local-history
256x8b + 4096x2b PHT plus 1-cycle recovery) cut cycles only 4,431,994 -> 4,378,139 (-1.2%), which is
exactly what the 1-cycle recovery alone is worth (~55K mispredicts x 1 cycle), i.e. the fancy direction
predictor bought ~0. The fetch-queue/skid decoupling variants (r3s2..r5s2, r8s2) all failed on Fmax.
The one control-flow class the current predictor never touches is the non-`ret` JALR. Only
`jalr x0,0(x1)` is predicted (RAS); every other JALR is an unconditional 2-cycle kill_q recovery.
CoreMark has two such sources: (1) the core_state_transition `switch(state)` jump table (`lw; add; jr a5`),
executed once per input character over ~3 passes of the ~666-byte state-machine input every iteration
(~2K indirect jumps/iter, and state runs are long: the same state repeats while digits/letters repeat, so
last-target is right most of the time), and (2) function-pointer calls (`jalr ra,0(a5)`) in the list
mergesort compare callback and similar, which always go to the same target within one call.
These are not predicted at all today, are not aliased by the BHT, and the direction predictor cannot
help them. Unlike the 1-cycle-recovery / bigger-PHT attempts, this touches no EX/ID critical cone:
the EX-side check (`jalr_hit = pred_taken && a_in == {pred_target,00}`) and the RAS-style recovery
already exist and are reused unchanged.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a tiny indirect-target cache (iBTB) to branch_predictor.sv and use it for JALR instructions that are
not `ret`, and whose immediate is 0 (instr[31:20]==0, which covers `jr aN` jump tables and `jalr ra,0(aN)`
indirect calls -- restricting to imm==0 keeps the EX compare as the existing `a_in == pred_target`, with no
adder in front of the compare and no new load on the forwarded `a_in` net).

Fetch side (branch_predictor.sv): predecode `is_ibtb = is_jalr_op && instr[31:20]==12'b0` (ret keeps
priority and still uses ras0). 16 entries x 18 bits (target word address pc[19:2]), `(* syn_ramstyle =
"distributed_ram" *)`/LUT-RAM, no reset, async read, index = pc[5:2] ^ pc[9:6] (XOR-fold to spread the few
hot jalr sites). Targets are stored as 18 bits so the predicted PC is always {12'b0, t18, 2'b00}: always
word aligned and inside the low 1 MiB even for an uninitialised/garbage entry, so a cold entry can never
produce an out-of-bounds fetch (invariant 6) -- a wrong hit costs exactly what an unpredicted JALR costs
today (the 2-cycle kill_q recovery), it is never a correctness issue because EX verifies every JALR
prediction. No valid bits (keeps the read cone to one RAM read + the existing pred_target mux).
pred_taken |= is_ibtb; pred_target = is_ret ? ras0 : is_ibtb ? {12'b0, btb_rd} : sum. RAS push on calls
(is_call already includes JALR with rd==x1) is unchanged.

Update side: update from the *MEM-stage* EX/MEM register, not from EX, so nothing is added to the
late EX cones. In core.sv (wires only), when ex_mem_w.valid && ex_mem_w.ctrl.is_jalr &&
!ex_mem_w.ctrl.is_illegal && ex_mem_w.instr[31:20]==0 && ex_mem_w.instr != 32'h0000_8067 &&
ex_mem_w.mem_addr[31:20]==0 (EX/MEM.mem_addr already holds a_in+imm = the JALR target from the dedicated
AGU adder, and is_illegal is set by the misalign trap so trapping jumps never train), write
btb[idx(ex_mem_w.pc)] <= ex_mem_w.mem_addr[19:2] through the same one-stage upd_*_q register used by the
BHT. Writes are idempotent, so re-issuing them during a dmem stall (EX/MEM held) is harmless; wrong-path
JALRs are bubbled before EX/MEM (valid=0) so they never train. `ret` is excluded so it cannot alias-pollute
a jump-table entry.

Everything on the EX side is untouched: a BTB-predicted JALR arrives in EX with pred_taken=1 and
pred_target = predicted target; `jalr_hit` compares a_in with it exactly like a RAS-predicted ret; a wrong
target recovers via the existing `recover_target` (jalr_sum, or pc+4 if misaligned) and the registered
kill_q path. Expected effect is purely cycles: each correctly predicted indirect jump saves the 2-cycle
kill_q penalty. Netlist cost is ~16x18 LUT-RAM bits (~5 RAM16s), a 3:1 instead of 2:1 pred_target mux,
one 12-bit zero detect on imem_data, and one small write port; no flop stage is added to any EX/MEM/ID
cone. If `make timing` shows the imem_data -> predecode -> pred_target -> pc path in the top group, the
fallback inside this hypothesis is to drop the XOR-fold (index pc[5:2] only) and shrink to 8 entries.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-003-r9s2 (regression, -0.70%): A 16x18b LUT-RAM last-target iBTB for non-`ret` `imm==0` JALR (jump-table `jr`, `jalr ra,0(aN)`, trained from EX/MEM `mem_addr`, EX check and `kill_q` recovery untouched) scored 223.75 vs the 225.33 champion, i.e. inside the ~10% seed spread, because the ceiling is only ~2K indirect jumps/iter x 2 saved cycles (~1% of cycles, the proposal's own +1% estimate) while it adds a 3:1 `pred_target` mux and an iBTB read on the imem_data -> predecode -> `pc` path, so no CoreMark control-flow class is left worth predicting at fetch — with direction (r6s2/r7s2), recovery-latency and now indirect-target predictors all at or below noise, stop predictor work and spend effort only on Fmax ideas backed by a `make timing` top-path report.

title: Pin the late operand sources (regfile read, wb_next) to one final LUT in the ID operand capture
motivation:
`make timing` on the champion (place option 0, 90.6 MHz, data delay ~11.0 ns
against a 5 ns constraint) shows two tied top groups, both ending in the
ID/EX op_b / rs2_val flops:
  (a) dmem BSRAM DO -> u_mem byte/half align + sign (4 LUTs, ~1.5 ns net after
      DO) -> wb_next_20 -> rs2_nxt_20_s24 -> rs2_nxt_20_s0 -> op_b_nxt_20_s0 -> D.
      wb_next passes THREE LUT levels in id_stage (s_early, rs2_nxt, then op_b_nxt
      re-using rs2_nxt because op_b == rs2_nxt whenever alu_src == 0).
  (b) imem_data[24] (the timed netlist wires io_imemData straight to the LFSR
      flop) -> sel2_wb/rs2_byp compare (2 LUTs, fan-out 8) -> s_use_rf
      (fan-out 32, one 3.0 ns net) -> enters the regfile read tree at its FIRST
      level (rs2_nxt_2_s19/I3) -> 4 more LUT levels of the read tree ->
      op_b_nxt_2_s0 -> D. The select that the source comment says is applied "at
      the very last 3-input mux" was folded by synthesis into the leaf of the
      32:1 read mux, so the late select sits in front of the deepest part of
      the cone, and the shared rs2_nxt -> op_b_nxt chaining adds another level.
Earlier attempts cut only one of these cones by re-pipelining the data (one-hot
lane flops, LUT-RAM regfile); the other group immediately became the limiter
(r7s0/r7s1/r8s0). Neither group needs a different pipeline: the late values
(regfile read data, wb_next) only need to be forced to enter the capture at the
LAST LUT, independently for op_a, op_b and rs2_val, which synthesis is not
doing by itself.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cycle-neutral, interface-neutral restructuring of the ID operand capture, with
explicit netlist boundaries so Gowin synthesis cannot re-fold the selects:
1. reg_file.sv / id_stage.sv: add `(* syn_keep = 1 *)` (and `keep`) on the
   regfile mux outputs rs1_raw / rs2_raw, so the 32:1 read tree is a hard
   boundary and nothing (select, alu_src, byp) can be merged into its leaves.
2. mem_stage.sv: same attribute on wb_next, so the byte/half align + mem_to_reg
   mux is one cone ending at a net that feeds only the capture LUTs.
3. id_stage.sv: replace the nested operand muxes by one-hot AND-OR with early
   masks, each operand an independent LUT5-class function of
   {late_wb_next, m_wb, late_rs_raw, m_rf, early_other}:
     m_wb_b   = !alu_src & sel2_wb                     (early: compare + decode)
     m_rf_b   = !alu_src & !sel2_wb & !rs2_byp
     early_b  = alu_src ? imm : (!sel2_wb & rs2_byp ? wb_data : 0)
     op_b_nxt = (wb_next & {32{m_wb_b}}) | (rs2_raw & {32{m_rf_b}}) | early_b
   and the same for op_a (auipc gating) and rs2_nxt (no alu_src term). op_b no
   longer reads rs2_nxt, so wb_next and rs2_raw each see exactly one LUT before
   the ID/EX flop, and the select fan-out (32 per mask) is driven from LUTs that
   only depend on the early compare outputs. Priority is unchanged (MEM-stage
   producer > WB-stage bypass > regfile), so forwarding behaviour and the
   ID/EX register contents are bit-identical; all other modules, ID/EX layout and
   EX/forward logic are untouched.
Expected effect: removes ~2 LUT levels (~1-1.5 ns incl. the fan-out net) from
both tied cones at once, which is what the single-cone attempts could not do,
without adding flops or fan-out (no replicated one-hot lane flops as in r9s0).
The risk is that placement noise (seeds 90.6-99.9 MHz) hides a ~5-8% gain, and
that EX/alu_result cones (not in the top-5 list but within ~1 ns) become the
next limiter.

title: Zero-wait direct-mapped I-cache in front of the imem bus: hits hide the ~22% imem stalls
motivation:
Every front-end/predictor/Fmax-cone idea tried since r6s1 is at or below the 225.33 champion
(r6s2/r7s2 direction predictors, r9s2 indirect-target cache, r3s2/r4s2/r5s2/r8s2 fetch queues,
r7s1/r8s0/r9s0 load-align and regfile cone cuts). LESSONS.md says direction/recovery/indirect
predictors are capped at ~2.5% of cycles, and the fetch queues only recover ~6% of cycles
(backend-stall serialisation) and give it back in Fmax. None of them touches the biggest
single cycle sink: the random ~22% imem backpressure. The timed CoreMark window is 2.92M
retired instructions in 4.43M cycles (CPI 1.51). A one-instruction-per-fetch front end at 78%
ready costs 2.92M/0.78 - 2.92M = ~0.82M cycles (about 18% of all cycles) before any backend
stall, and the core pays it on every fetch because it has no local instruction storage.
Measured, not guessed: I built bench/programs/coremark.elf (-O3, TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=2000), ran
it through test/cosim/reference.py (the Python ISS) and replayed the 2,922,015 retired PCs
between the 0x10000100/0x10000104 markers through a direct-mapped cache model. The timed
window touches only 1,669 distinct instruction words (~6.7 KB). Cold-start misses included,
hit rate is 83.3% (128 lines), 93.8% (256 lines), 97.0% (512 lines, 2 KB), 98.9% (1024
lines, 4 KB), 99.4% (2048 lines). A small direct-mapped I-cache inside the core can therefore
serve almost every fetch without touching the bus. ARCHITECTURE.md/CLAUDE.md allow adding
caches, and the fitness text says stall-hiding logic is part of the timed circuit (it is
charged area and Fmax), so this is a legitimate microarchitecture feature, not an eval
relaxation.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/icache.sv, a direct-mapped, read-only instruction cache between the PC and the imem
bus, and make if_stage fetch through it. Stores are not snooped (CoreMark does not modify
code; FENCE.I stays an architectural NOP as today).

Structure (the simplest thing that can hit with zero bubbles):
  * 512 lines (97.0% measured hit rate) as the default; 1024 lines (98.9%) if timing allows;
    256 lines (93.8%) is the fallback if the LUT-RAM read cone is the limiter. Index = low
    pc word bits, tag = the remaining pc[19:..] bits (addresses are bounded to the low
    1 MiB, so the tag is ~9 bits), one valid bit per line.
  * Data and tag arrays are asynchronous-read distributed RAM
    (`syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram"`, the style r8s0 already got through Gowin and
    formal), read with the PC flop as the address. A hit delivers the instruction in the
    same cycle as today's imem_data, so the combinational IF/ID bundle, the predecode/BHT/RAS
    predictor and the ID cones are unchanged apart from one 2:1
    `fetch_instr = hit ? ic_data : imem_data` select in if_stage.
  * `fetch_ok = hit || io_imemReady` replaces io_imemReady in hazard_unit (stall_if /
    flush_if) and in the `fire` input of branch_predictor, so a hit never stalls or injects
    a NOP. A miss behaves exactly like today (hold PC, NOP into ID until the bus delivers).
  * Fill: when the bus delivers (io_imemReady) for a missing line, write {tag, instr} on that
    clock edge. The write data is the raw imem word, so there is no new logic on the fetch
    cone. A wrong-path miss that fills is harmless.
  * Validity without a 512:1 valid mux: after reset a small sweep counter clears the
    valid/tag RAM entry by entry while `hit` is forced to 0 and fills are suppressed. The
    core runs from the bus meanwhile, with no stall, and the sweep (512 cycles) ends long
    before the CoreMark start marker. Alternative: valid flops with a 256-line cache.
    riscv-formal's short BMC depth then never sees a hit, so the formal contract is
    unchanged and the cosim CoreMark run (CRC-checked, ~97% hits) is what exercises the hit
    path. Do not use memory `initial` values: r8s1 showed they make the formal solver time
    out.
  * RVFI-visible behaviour is unchanged: same instruction sequence and same
    pc/order/trap reporting; only the cycle at which an instruction is delivered changes.

Expected effect: removing most of the ~0.82M-cycle imem-stall term (at 97% hits, minus the
part that overlaps backend stalls) should cut total cycles by roughly 12-18%, i.e. about
+14-22% iterations/cycle. That beats the 4.6% bar even if Fmax gives back 8-10%. The added
cone is pc flop -> LUT-RAM read -> tag compare -> hit -> {fetch_instr select,
stall_if/flush_if}. Unlike the r5s2/r8s2 queues it adds no head mux in front of the ID
regfile-read/forward-select cone beyond that one 2:1 select, and it does not change the
mispredict penalty (still the registered 2-cycle kill_q recovery). If `make timing` shows the
hit compare or the instruction select in the top paths, the fallbacks are to store a
pre-decoded predictor hint with each line (taken/target computed at fill time) so the
predictor adder is off the hit path, or to shrink the cache to 256 lines.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-002-r10s1 (regression, -43.44%): A zero-wait direct-mapped distributed-RAM I-cache whose hit path (pc flop -> LUT-RAM read -> tag compare -> `hit` -> `fetch_instr = hit ? ic_data : imem_data`) fed the regfile read addresses, hazard-unit load-use compares, predecode/BHT/RAS and `stall_if`/`flush_if` scored 127.45 vs the 225.33 champion, and since a hit never adds a stall and a miss behaves as before cycles cannot have risen, so the whole loss (far beyond the 8-10% Fmax give-back budgeted against a 12-18% cycle gain) is Fmax from putting a RAM read, compare and 2:1 select in series ahead of the existing ~16 ns ID cones, which had treated `imem_data` as an early-arriving bus input — hiding the ~22% imem stalls with local instruction storage is not viable here unless the cache output is registered before ID (the F/D-stage version r8s2 also lost), so with queues and cache both failed treat imem-stall hiding as exhausted.

title: Tournament direction predictor: 256x2b bimodal, 1024x2b gshare, 256x2b chooser
motivation:
Prior predictor attempts here fixed the front end (fetch queues, skid stage,
1-cycle recovery), added a per-branch local-history table (r6s2/r7s2) or an
indirect-target cache (r9s2). Only the 128x2b pc[8:2]-indexed bimodal table
has survived. I profiled the CoreMark 2K -O3 binary on the Python ISS
(2.94M insns, 532K conditional branches, 13.8K rets, only 22 non-ret JALRs)
and replayed the branch trace through candidate predictors. Mispredicts of
the current 128x2b bimodal: 54.9K (10.3% of branches) = 110K cycles at the
2-cycle penalty = 2.5% of the ~4.43M cycles, matching the earlier lesson.
Replayed alternatives: bimodal 256: 44.7K; bimodal 1024+: ~40K (aliasing
accounts for ~15K, the rest is data-dependent branches no table fixes);
gshare 2048/h11: 36.8K; tournament (256 bimodal + 512 gshare h9 + 256
chooser): 34.1K; tournament (256 + 1024 gshare h10): 29.7K; local-history
256x8/2048 (the r6s2 style): 27.5K. So direction accuracy is worth at most
1.2% of cycles, and the tournament captures about 1.1% of it. It is cheaper
to build than the local-history design and keeps all state in the same
fetch-time LUT-RAM read structure, off the imem_data -> pc path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the single 128x2b bimodal table in branch_predictor.sv with a small
tournament predictor held in no-reset LUT-RAM (performance-only state):
(a) bimodal table, 256 entries indexed by pc[9:2] (cuts aliasing: 54.9K ->

10-bit global history register (GHR), (c) a 256x2b chooser indexed by

disagree. The GHR is shifted at fetch (only when `fire`, for predicted
conditional branches, with the predicted direction) and repaired on a
mispredict from a 10-bit snapshot carried in ID/EX: on kill, GHR is loaded
with {snapshot[8:0], actual_direction}. The reads for all three tables
start from the pc and GHR flops, so they run in parallel with the imem_data
predecode/19-bit target adder and only join at the final pred_taken AND.

instead of the current 2-bit bht_cnt) are carried down the pipe and
written back through the existing registered EX update stage (one cycle
after EX), so the late branch compare still only reaches flop D pins. The
mispredict check, kill_q recovery, RAS and JAL handling are unchanged, so
correctness, RVFI and formal are unaffected. Expected gain is the
~20K-mispredict reduction (about 1% of cycles) at near-zero Fmax cost. This

fetch-side predictor logic is not in any recent top-N timing path, so the
change stays Fmax-neutral and any accepted result comes from the cycle gain
plus place-and-route variance. Confidence is low.

title: Unreset LUT-RAM regfile with x0 address-detect zeroing (no written-bit flops)
motivation:
The best Fmax distribution seen so far came from r8s0, which swapped the 31x32
fabric-flop regfile and its two 32:1 flop read muxes for two distributed-RAM
arrays plus a 31-flop `written` zero-gate. It scored 102.4 / 102.4 / 99.3 MHz
over the three placement options (champion: 99.9 / 99.9 / 90.6) with 2860 LUT4
and 878 FF (champion: 3965 / 1839), and the top path dropped from 8-9 to 8
logic cells. It still lost, because the champion's median is one lucky
placement and the gain over it was only +2.5%. The r8s0 notes say Fmax is
routing-dominated and the three ~10 ns cones (BSRAM DO -> u_mem -> u_id, regfile
read -> u_id, EX forward -> ALU -> alu_result) are tied, so the lever with a
measured effect is netlist size and fan-out, not LUT-level shuffling. r8s0 still
carries avoidable logic: 31 `written` flops, their per-register write decode,
and a 31:1 mux of those bits in parallel with each LUT-RAM read. That mux sits
on the regfile -> ID/EX operand-capture cone, the same cone where r8s0's worst
path ended.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rewrite reg_file.sv (ports unchanged, so core.sv, id_stage.sv and the cocotb
tests are untouched) as two distributed-RAM arrays, one per read port. Both are
32x32 with `syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram"`, written in parallel at
{w_addr, w_data} under `w_nz`. There is NO reset and NO `initial` value, and no
`written` bit vector. x0 is zeroed only by a 5-bit address-zero detect:
rs*_raw = (rs*_addr == 0) ? 0 : ram[rs*_addr]. That detect is a parallel NOR5
that folds into the single LUT after the RAM read, instead of a 31:1 mux of
flop bits. Write-first bypass (rs*_byp = w_nz && w_addr == rs*_addr) is kept
bit-exact, as are the `rs*_raw` / `rs*_byp` outputs that id_stage already
folds into the operand capture.

Why dropping the reset and `written` bits is architecturally safe:
  - CoreMark's crt0 writes sp/gp/etc. before any use, and the gcc-generated code
    never reads a register it has not written.
  - Gowin SSRAM powers up as 0 and Verilator zero-initialises arrays, so the
    cosim against reference.py (initial regs 0) stays identical.
  - riscv-formal's `reg` check treats never-written registers as unconstrained.
    The x0 checks only need rs1/rs2_rdata == 0 for address 0, which the detect
    guarantees.
  - Do NOT use an `initial` zero-fill loop. r8s1 showed that makes smtbmc carry
    constant-initialised arrays and blows the formal time budget. r8s0's plain
    uninitialised array finished formal.

Expected effect: about 31 fewer FFs plus ~60 LUTs vs r8s0, one fewer LUT level
on the regfile read -> `op_a`/`op_b`/`rs2_val` capture cone, and ~1000 fewer
flops/LUTs than the champion. Cycle count is identical (4,431,994), so
fitness moves only through Fmax. The aim is to keep r8s0's tight 99-102 MHz
placement spread and tilt it up by removing the one remaining regfile-side
gate. If `make timing` still shows BSRAM -> u_mem -> u_id as the sole top
path, the result is expected to be about r8s0's 231 (inside the 4.6% noise
band). The upside case is the 3-seed median reaching ~104-106 MHz.

Keep ports and the write-first bypass flags (rs*_byp) and rs*_data/rs*_raw outputs bit-identical so id_stage/core are untouched.

title: Registered-output I-cache with predecode hints feeding a real F/D flop stage (fetch loop isolated from ID cones)
motivation:
Cycles, not cones, are the only large lever left. CoreMark retires ~2.92M instructions in
4.43M cycles (CPI 1.51). About 0.82M cycles are the random ~22% imem backpressure, and the
core has no local instruction storage, so it pays that on every fetch. Every other cycle
idea (direction/indirect predictors, recovery latency, fetch queues) is capped at ~1-2.5%,
and the Fmax-cone rewrites are exhausted at the ~16 ns floor.
r10s1 measured the cache upper bound: a direct-mapped I-cache served ~97% of fetches and
cut cycles 4.43M -> 3.64M (+21.8% iterations/cycle, formal and cosim clean). It lost only
because Fmax fell to 46 MHz. Its critical path (25.9 ns, 22 cells) went
pc -> u_ic (RAM read + tag compare + `hit`) -> `hit ? ic_data : imem_data` -> hazard_unit /
u_id (regfile read, load-use, forward selects) -> back into u_if / u_bp. The cache output
was combinational into ID, so the RAM read, compare and select were stacked in front of
the existing ~16 ns ID cones. r8s2 showed that a real F/D flop stage plus skid costs only
~4.5% Fmax (95.4 vs 99.9 MHz, inside the seed spread) and ID reads from flops. Nobody has
combined the two. Needed: a cache whose output is registered into F/D, so the hit path
never reaches ID, and whose predictor hint is precomputed at fill time, so the only new
loop is short.
Break-even for the +4.6% acceptance bar: ~+19% iterations/cycle (cache at ~3.7M cycles
after the +1 mispredict cycle) needs Fmax >= ~88 MHz, i.e. a give-back of at most ~12%.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small direct-mapped read-only I-cache and make if_stage a true two-step fetch -> F/D
flop stage. Hits deliver an instruction every cycle regardless of imem_ready, and ID/regfile/
hazard/forward logic reads F/D flops only (same launch point as today's imem_data flop in
the timed netlist).

1. rtl/icache.sv (new): 256 lines (93.8% hit in r10s1's replay; 512 lines = 97% if the
   LUT count and timing allow) indexed by fpc[9:2], async-read distributed RAM
   (syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram", the style r8s0 got through Gowin and formal). Each
   line holds {tag, 32-bit instruction, predecode hint}. The hint is computed at FILL time
   from the raw bus word (imem_data -> predecode -> 19-bit adder -> RAM write data; this ends
   at a RAM write port, not in the fetch loop): kind {none, jal, branch, ret}, is_call, and
   the static 19-bit target (pc + J/B imm, with static_ok / alignment / 1 MiB-range already
   folded into kind=none). Fill: whenever the bus delivers (imem_ready) for fpc and it is a
   miss, write the line, even when F/D is held, so the cache doubles as the skid buffer
   (a held fetch is refetched as a hit). Validity: reset sweep that clears the valid/tag
   entries one per cycle while hit is forced 0 and fills are suppressed (about 256 cycles,
   long before the CoreMark start marker). No memory `initial` values (r8s1: smtbmc timeout)
   and no wide valid-flop mux. Formal's short BMC never sees a hit, so the contract is
   unchanged; cosim CoreMark exercises the hit path. Stores are not snooped; FENCE.I stays
   an architectural NOP.

2. rtl/if_stage.sv: the combinational IF/ID bundle becomes a real F/D register
   {pc, instr, valid, pred_taken, pred_target, bht_cnt}.
     f_hit = icache hit at fpc; f_ok = f_hit || imem_ready
     f_instr = f_hit ? c_data : imem_data   (feeds only the F/D flops, not ID)
     F/D <= {fpc, f_instr, valid=1, pred} when f_ok && !hold && !kill
     F/D <= NOP (0x00000013), valid=0 on a miss without bus data, or on kill
     fpc <= kill ? kill_target : (!hold && f_ok) ? next_fpc : fpc
   where hold = load-use || dmem stall || mdu stall (imem_ready is no longer in the hold).
   imem_addr stays the fpc flop. Stalled/NOP F/D slots carry the NOP instruction so
   decode of a bubble is benign (ex_stage's EX/MEM ctrl capture is not gated by valid).

3. rtl/branch_predictor.sv: on a hit the next-fpc select uses the stored hint
   (taken = kind==jal | kind==ret | kind==branch & bht_cnt[1]; target = ret ? ras0 : hint
   target), so the hit loop is fpc -> LUT-RAM read -> tag compare -> hit & kind decode ->
   19-bit next_fpc mux -> fpc, with no adder and no opcode compare. On a miss the front end
   does not follow a prediction (pred_taken=0; EX recovers as it already does for
   unpredicted JAL/branches). RAS push/pop on a miss still uses a predecode of the raw bus
   word (that path ends at the RAS flops only). BHT/RAS read/update and the registered EX
   BHT-update stage are unchanged. EX's prediction check and kill_q recovery are untouched.

4. rtl/hazard_unit.sv, rtl/core.sv, rtl/id_stage.sv: regfile read addresses, load-use
   compare and forward-select inputs come from the F/D instr flops (not io_imemData);
   imem_ready is removed from stall_if/flush_if, `kill` flushes the F/D slot and the ID/EX
   bubble as today. Mispredict recovery becomes 3 cycles instead of 2 (+~55K cycles,
   ~1.2%), already included in the estimate. RVFI reporting is unchanged.

Expected cycles ~3.70-3.75M vs 4.43M (+18-20% iterations/cycle). The fitness gain depends
on Fmax holding at >= ~88 MHz. New loops are short and isolated from ID, whose cones stay at
the same ~16 ns, and the F/D stage alone costs ~0 to -4.5% (r8s2). If the timing report
shows the RAM read / tag compare, shrink to 256 lines (default) or store the tag compare
result per line index in a narrower tag. If LUT4 count gets high (the line is ~65 bits x 256
= ~1000 RAM16 LUTs plus read muxes; the 10000 target gives ample headroom), drop the hint
target and recompute pc+imm from the cached instruction in the F/D stage.

title: Train the BHT from registered pred_taken ^ kill_q instead of the EX branch compare, removing the compare -> upd_taken_q endpoint
motivation:
Every predictor lever that changes prediction quality or recovery latency has been
measured here and sits at or below place-and-route noise. From the replayed CoreMark
trace (2.94M retired insns, 55K mispredicts = 110K of 4.43M cycles = 2.5%), the
direction ceiling is ~1.2% (r10s2), the indirect-target ceiling ~1% (r9s2), and the
1-cycle recovery ceiling ~1.2% (r7s2). The remaining 3.77M of the 4.43M cycles are the
22%-imem-stall fetch bound, which fetch-side decoupling (r3s2..r5s2, r8s2) and the
I-cache (r10s1) failed to hide at this clock. So the remaining predictor angle is not
accuracy. It is the predictor's own contribution to the timed critical cones.
The champion's top-path reports repeatedly end at predictor flops: r4s1 and r10s0 both
have a 15.9-18.6 ns path ID/EX op_a -> forward mux -> branch compare ->
u_if/u_bp/upd_taken_q (36 cells), and r4s0 ended at kill_q. The 32-bit branch compare
result `branch_cond` therefore has TWO late endpoints: the kill_q D pin (needed) and the
BHT-training flop upd_taken_q (not needed, because the BHT is performance-only and is
written one cycle later anyway). The second endpoint adds fan-out on the compare's final
LUT and on the shared a_in/s_in nets feeding the compare chain.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Remove the late EX compare as a BHT training source and reconstruct the resolved
direction one cycle later from state that is already registered.
For a branch that leaves EX on a non-wrong-path cycle (exactly the cycles where
bht_upd_valid is set), kill_q is loaded with `mispredict`, and for a branch
mispredict == (branch_cond != in.pred_taken). So in the following cycle, when
upd_we_q is high, the resolved direction is
    upd_taken_q = upd_pred_q ^ kill_q
where upd_pred_q is in.pred_taken registered together with upd_idx_q/upd_cnt_q.
kill_q cannot be high for any other reason in that cycle: bht_upd_valid already
requires !kill_q, so kill_q(t+1) = bht_upd_valid(t) && mispredict(t). The only case where
the derived direction differs from branch_cond is an unpredicted taken branch with a
misaligned target, where mispredict is suppressed and the trap fires. There the BHT
trains not-taken, which affects performance only. The BHT counter update
(upd_new = sat_inc/dec(upd_cnt_q, upd_taken_q)) then runs entirely from flops
(kill_q, upd_pred_q, upd_cnt_q) into the LUT-RAM write data, off the EX compare cone.
Concrete edits:
  - ex_stage.sv: drop the bht_upd_taken output (= branch_cond) and export
    bht_upd_pred = in.pred_taken in its place. bht_upd_valid, bht_upd_idx and
    bht_upd_cnt stay as they are. kill_q and kill_target_q are untouched, so the
    mispredict -> kill_q cone loses its only sibling endpoint.
  - branch_predictor.sv: register upd_pred_q next to upd_idx_q, add a `kill` input, and
    compute upd_taken_q = upd_pred_q ^ kill. The reset-free upd_*_q data flops and the
    reset-only upd_we_q are unchanged. The BHT array, RAS, predecode, static-target adder,
    pred_target and the pc -> next_pc path are not touched, so the fetch path gets no new
    logic (r7s2/r9s2/r10s2 all regressed by adding logic there).
  - if_stage.sv and core.sv: rename the bht_upd_taken wire to bht_upd_pred and pass the
    existing kill wire into the predictor. No other behavioural change.
Cycle count is bit-identical to the champion in all but the misaligned-taken-branch
corner, which CoreMark never executes. RVFI, trap discipline, kill_q recovery and
formal behaviour are unchanged, since the BHT is not architecturally visible.
Expected effect: the compare cone ends only at kill_q. This is the same trick as the
earlier "decouple the late endpoint" wins (r4s1: BSRAM-address and CE/SR fan-out
decoupling, +11.9%), applied to the last remaining sibling endpoint. Honest estimate:
a small Fmax gain (~1-3%) with the ~10% place-and-route seed spread as a caveat. It is cycle-neutral and
removes ~2 FFs and a LUT. Judge it by whether `make timing` still shows
upd_taken_q as a top endpoint on the baseline and not on the candidate. Do not add
anything to the pc -> predecode -> next_pc path while implementing it.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-003-r11s2 (regression, +2.04%): Training the BHT from registered `upd_pred_q ^ kill_q` instead of the EX `branch_cond` (cycle-neutral, ~2 FFs and a LUT fewer, `upd_taken_q` removed as a compare endpoint) scored 229.93 vs the 225.33 champion, inside the ~10% place-and-route seed spread and short of the +1-3% hoped-for gain being distinguishable, even though r4s1/r10s0 top-path reports ended at `upd_taken_q` — the sibling endpoint only added one D-pin load, while the forward mux -> 32-bit compare chain that still feeds `kill_q` (and ties with regfile -> ALU -> `alu_result` at ~16-18 ns) is the real limiter, so dropping a duplicate endpoint of a cone does not shorten the cone; only a change that cuts the shared source chain itself (or a measured `make timing` shift of the top endpoint) can pay, and predictor-side endpoint trimming is exhausted.

title: Per-byte-lane replicated select/decode nets in the regfile read and load-align cones
motivation:
A fresh `make timing` on the champion (90.6 MHz placement, 11.0 ns launch-to-capture) shows the top
paths are routing-dominated, not LUT-depth-dominated. Path 3 (imem bit lfsr_24 -> regfile read -> ID/EX
op_b) spends 3.03 ns on ONE net: the fanout-32 select/decode LUT (rs2_nxt_27_s25) that has to reach
every one of the 32 bit-slices of the 32:1 read mux, which Gowin places far apart; 5 more LUT levels
follow, with ~0.3-0.9 ns nets each. Path 1 (BSRAM DO[7] -> u_mem -> u_id op_b) has 5.5 ns of nets out of
8.7 ns after the BSRAM: a fanout-16 sign-extension net (wb_next_Z_31_s0), then a fanout-3 and 1.23 ns hop
into the capture mux. Earlier rounds removed LUT levels (one-hot lanes, capture rewrites, LUT-RAM
regfile) and landed within noise because the tied cones were each still bounded by a single
wide-fanout select net; nobody has split those nets per byte lane. r2s0's +32% came from exactly
this kind of fan-out trim on the redirect net.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replicate the wide select logic in the two top cones so no select net drives more than 8 bit-slices,
keeping every function identical (cycle count unchanged).
(1) reg_file.sv / id_stage.sv: for each read port build the one-hot address decode once per byte lane
(4 copies, each (* syn_keep = 1 *) so Gowin cannot merge them) and form rs*_raw as an explicit AND-OR
over the 31 registers (x0 simply has no term) using that lane's own decode, so each decode wire fans out to
8 bits instead of 32. The AND-OR is 1.5 levels of decode + 3 levels of LUT4 (AND2-OR2 / OR4 / OR4)
instead of the current 2 decode + 5 mux levels. Replicate the registered-source selects of the capture
mux (a_use_rf/b_use_rf/s_use_rf, which are functions of imem bits, rs*_byp and sel*_wb) the same way, one copy
per byte lane.
(2) mem_stage.sv: compute the load sign bit and the lane/width select terms once per byte lane of
the upper half-word (copies for bits [31:24], [23:16], [15:8], with syn_keep) rather than one
sign net with fanout 16, so each copy drives 8 loads of the wb_next mux and the ID capture.
Cost: roughly 4x32 decode LUTs per read port (~250 LUT4 total, ~6% of 3965) and a few extra loads on the
imem address bits, which in the timed netlist are LFSR flops with spare slack on the first hop. Estimated
gain: ~1.5 ns off the ID cone and ~1 ns off the load cone on an 11 ns path, i.e. ~6% Fmax if both
cones move together (they are the two worst groups, tied within 0.02 ns). Risk: the EX forward ->
ALU and kill_q cones sit only ~0.25 ns behind (10.78 ns) and the ~10% place-and-route seed spread; the
design intent here is to remove the single biggest net in each of the two worst cones.

lesson: - 2026-10-03 hyp-20261003-001-r12s0 (regression, +4.07%): Replicating the wide select nets per byte lane with `syn_keep` (4 regfile read decodes, per-lane `a_/b_/s_use_rf` capture selects and `rs*_byp`, per-lane load sign/lane-select terms in `mem_stage`) was cycle-neutral and scored 234.49 vs the 225.33 champion, about +4% against the +6% estimated and inside the ~10% place-and-route seed spread (r6s1 itself ran 90.6-99.9 MHz), so cutting the fanout-32 / fanout-16 select nets to fanout 8 did not demonstrably move Fmax — the replicas add ~250 LUTs and 4x load on the shared imem-address/`rs*_byp`/`mem_addr` sources, so the ~3 ns hop looks like placement distance across the BSRAM/regfile bit-slices rather than fanout itself; select-net replication joins the exhausted capture/load-align/regfile rewrites (r7s1, r9s0, r10s0, r11s0), so only retry with a seed-averaged `make timing` showing that specific net's delay drop.

title: Registered-output I-cache with hit-free fetch loop (optimistic next-fpc from cached hint, tag compare verified one stage late in F/D)
motivation:
The only structural lever that has ever beaten the champion's cycle count is local instruction
storage. r10s1 measured the cache upper bound (~97% of fetches served, cycles 4.43M -> 3.64M,
+21.8% iter/cycle) but lost 43% because the cache output was combinational into ID. r11s1 fixed
that by registering the cache output into a real F/D flop stage: cycles 3.74M (+18.4% iter/cycle),
formal and cosim clean, fitness 234.56 (+4.10%, just under the +4.6% bar) with Fmax 87.67 MHz
vs the champion's 99.87. Its measured worst path (make timing, 17.94 ns, 20 cells, 10 levels)
is NOT in ID any more. It is the new fetch loop:
  fpc_5 -> u_ic (LUT-RAM read + tag compare = hit) -> u_if (f_ok / hit gating) -> u_bp
  (pred_taken/target select) -> u_if (next_fpc mux + fpc clock enable) -> fpc_18.
The ID cones are still at the ~16 ns floor, so removing the tag compare / `hit` / `f_ok` terms
(about 3-5 LUT levels, plus the high-fanout `hit` net into the fpc CE) from this loop is worth
up to ~+10-14% Fmax (87.7 -> ~95-99 MHz) on top of the +18% cycle gain. Both halves of the
r11s1 trade-off (cycles +18%, Fmax -12%) were already measured, so the expected value is the
product: ~+5-14% over the champion, comfortably over the acceptance bar if the loop gets under
~15 ns. This is a structural change to the fetch pipeline (which signals are allowed into the
fpc loop and which are verified a stage later), not a cone rewrite or a predictor tweak.
